Through numerical examples, the efficacy of our proposed method has been demonstrated. Additionally, the model's properties have been analyzed to provide contextual insight.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which circulation patterns are mapped and classified. Notable patterns and trends emerge when varying rotation rate, as well as the rate at which heat and motion are transferred and released in the atmosphere. Additionally, we find that there is a critical point at which the atmosphere begins to make multiple complete rotations within a day, and that above this point the atmosphere starts to move in opposite directions at different latitudes. We also observe that in the case of fast rotation, the atmosphere moves in the opposite direction to what is expected and begins to move in a random and complex pattern.

Our research involves creating a library for efficient neural network training that is
well-suited for large image classification tasks. Neural network architectures have
evolved significantly over time, and our aim is to understand how to choose the
best corresponding learning processes that are optimized for various computing resources.
We developed the PyLearn2 library to explore and evaluate different learning processes
and discovered that, for the large ImageNet dataset, the Nesterov Accelerated Gradient
descent learning process yields the best results among the processes we tested.
Our findings and the Nesterov Accelerated Gradient descent learning process are currently
being used in the Google Brain team.

Researchers who utilize silicon donor spin have explored approaches for realizing large-scale quantum computations. To advance these computations, it is crucial to incorporate functional units that feature exchange-coupled, paired quantum bits. In this study, an existing numerical simulation model, based on a multi-valley effective mass theory, has been expanded to accommodate two distant donors through the inclusion of electric field effects on the valley distribution. By leveraging this model, exchange-coupling in paired quantum bits has been demonstrated and its sensitivity to valley distribution has been examined. In addition, calculations of the optical absorption associated with the transition between a singlet state and a triplet state have been performed and the results obtained are comparable to prior findings reported by other researchers.

Our investigation focused on the conductance of an individual HgTe quantum well layer within a junction, particularly under dark conditions. We obtained clear and comprehensive data sets for both positive and negative magnetic fields. When the Fermi level was positioned near the neutral point, we observed unique conductance behavior in both the classical Coulomb blockade regime and the quantum Hall effect regime. Our research revealed the presence of highly conductive neutral states within the HgTe junction. We established a relationship between conductance and magnetic field based on theoretical models, using a single parameter that represents the width of the neutral region. Our findings also included the detection of highly localized neutral states within CdTe quantum well layers made from the same material. We achieved this by incorporating a small amount of Hg (approximately 1%) into the CdTe wells.

A proposed dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD) framework, known as Game-Theoretic Model Scheduling (GMS), is presented with predicted performance benefits. The GMS model is anticipated to provide optimized TDD configurations on a short time scale. Theoretical analysis indicates that the optimal strategy under the GMS model yields a threshold-based policy, allowing for the derivation of efficient offline schemes for result prediction and value function approximation. Through simulation testing with realistic 5G scenarios, the benefits of the GMS model were demonstrated across various performance metrics for both small and large datasets.

In this work, we introduce a novel understanding of Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) through the lens of dynamical systems. By reinterpreting HNNs in this context, we discover a precise and explicit formula for their derivative-based activations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that HNNs are equivalent to a specific class of recurrent neural networks that utilize derivative-based activations. To illustrate the benefits of this HNNs' characterization, we show that it yields a meaningful explanation for a notable training instability issue often encountered with standard HNNs.

Our proposed approach involves creating a collaborative environment among multiple agents, including a machine learning model and humans, working together to enhance the model's reliability by reviewing and refining its predictions and learning from feedback. The model scores each individual's trustworthiness, uses feedback to validate its insights, and employs data enhancement techniques based on anomalous instances. Our algorithm operates in a dynamic way, with each agent adapting to changes in the data and model dynamics. With the goal of developing a versatile framework, we divided our approach into three distinct variations of the algorithm. Our empirical studies using real-world data from a self-driving technology institution and a medical diagnostic dataset demonstrate notable increases in model performance, with improvements of up to 25% in accuracy and 50% in overall trustworthiness.

A newly defined topological invariant, reflected in the volume hypothesis, is established for a specific polynomial associated with links in a torus-knot network. The proposed polynomial, referred to as the Eichler invariant, is demonstrated to possess desirable properties, including a deterministic relationship with junctions of torus-knots and a predictable response to modifications made to links. Furthermore, the Eichler invariant is found to exhibit volume hypothesis behavior when coupled with the proposed network topology. Notably, the proposed relationship between the Eichler invariant and volume hypothesis behavior has been computationally verified for a limited range of links in the torus-knot network.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context. The existing state-of-the-art approaches rely heavily on neural networks, specifically BERT, which achieve superior performance due to their ability to incorporate contextual information effectively. Nonetheless, the limited availability of context-gloss pairs hinders the development of high-quality models, as they rely on manual annotations that are both time-consuming and costly to obtain. We present a novel strategy, Context-Gloss Augmentation (CGA), which leverages context-gloss pairs by creating synthetic instances through sentence substitutions. We demonstrate the efficacy of CGA in enhancing WSD results using a specially designed dataset containing multiple senses per word. Furthermore, we integrate CGA into a benchmark dataset consisting of nine words with a single sense each, and show that it yields a significant boost in performance. Our code is publicly accessible at the following link: https://github.com/ghali/Context-Gloss-Augmentation.

This study formulates a pair of regularized integral expressions representing the reciprocal Gamma function, leveraging the concept of Hadamard finite parts integrals. By utilizing these expressions, we derive a range of equivalent forms, including a double integral representation that can be used to further define the function for negative values typically excluded in the original Gamma function definition.

Using 150 - 300 pb of data from LHC proton-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV, ATLAS and CMS have implemented innovative methods to identify top quark production, specifically via the decay of top quarks into charged leptons and D mesons. These detections are crucial proof of top quark production in proton-lead collisions and facilitate further studies on heavy ion collisions.

This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL semantic interpretation, specifically schema linking and value retrieval. To enhance the effectiveness of schema linking, we propose using a column-type prediction pre-training model to facilitate the transfer learning in a linear layer. Furthermore, we suggest using two value retrieval methods: a flat set-based approach and a hierarchical method that leverages tree structures. The evaluation of these strategies on the Spider dataset shows improved performance compared to existing techniques. Our proposed framework, after parameter-free pre-training, achieves an F1 score of 20.3% on the validation set and 21.5% on the test set for the schema linking task and an average F1 score of 17.8% across all tables for the value retrieval task.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the context of multi-dimensional data that is characterized by its complex and varied structure. It outlines the difficulties encountered when applying differential privacy to such data, followed by an in-depth examination of established techniques for providing differential privacy for specific data structures. Additionally, it reviews innovations in methodologies that address various data structures, including those with multi-dimensional characteristics. A category of techniques applicable to broadly defined data structures is also explored. The paper also examines the application of differential privacy within specific domains such as graph, genetic, and recommender system data. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges faced when operating within networked data structures and possible approaches to their incorporation. Finally, it identifies key research directions within this domain.

The vast images and data generated by Euclid, with its high sensitivity and broad spectral range, will significantly influence the historical understanding of galaxies, galaxies' evolution, and the makeup of dark matter and energy. By analyzing data from the wide and shallow survey fields, Euclid will deliver critical insights into the distribution and movement of dark matter and energy across the cosmos. Through the deep survey in the most remote regions of the spectrum, Euclid will find some of the most distant galaxies ever spotted, providing invaluable information about the early development of the universe. By studying stars in the Milky Way and nearby galaxies, Euclid will gather detailed information about the formation and evolution of galaxies. Furthermore, Euclid will identify exoplanets that could support life and offer valuable data on the properties of dark matter and energy.

Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to model complex dynamics in quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel hydrodynamic approach for a wide range of interacting Bose gases within the range of weak interactions. Our method, which is based on a random phase-space approach, allows us to describe the dynamics of these systems through a set of easily interpretable hydrodynamic equations with both local and non-local characteristics. By matching our approach to the underlying microscopic physics, we've established a clear connection to the coefficients of specific hydrodynamic coefficients and scattering lengths within the range of weak interactions. Furthermore, our predictions have been tested against existing numerical results as well as experimental data from JILA and STAG experiments.

Consider a sequence of letters from a given alphabet, arranged in a specific order, where the distances between identical letters are measured along the sequence. Under the assumption that these distances behave asymptotically like a random variable as the sequence length increases, we establish two main results regarding the asymptotic probability of occurrence of letter configurations in the sequence. Firstly, for a fixed random reference, we prove that the asymptotic probability of a specific letter configuration behaves proportionally to the sequence length, while accounting for the expected sum of the asymptotic random variables. Secondly, we show that the asymptotic probability of a specific letter configuration varies proportionally to the sequence length, even when the random reference is itself a variable that evolves with the sequence length. In the latter case, we establish the proportionality up to a certain point, following the proof of a related average current zero-point fluctuation theorem.

We define a new concept of surface within a surface in the context of an abstract metric space, specifically inside the class of surfaces that map continuously to another surface without tearing, denoted as $H_0(S^2, H_0(\Sigma_0, \theta_0))$. Within this context, we prove that a surface that minimally covers another surface, through a mapping that respects the homotopy class, is itself the minimum energy surface within that homotopy class. Additionally, when the underlying space is smooth and the surface in question is smooth and area-minimizing, we establish that it belongs to a specific type of surface known as a minimal surface with bounded topological index.

Recent studies below 1 GeV using the IMP prompt neutron detector at the HIRU heavy-ion accelerator facility in China have made significant advancements in detecting shape coexistence in 64Ni. This nucleus, with a double closed shell configuration, has been found to exhibit a distinctive structure where the ground state and a 0+ excited state at 1253.4 keV possess a 4-particle, 4-hole configuration in the omega shell. Further research has been conducted using the GDR spectrum and giant monopole resonance data, allowing for a determination of inelastic scattering cross sections from 64Ni. These results, in conjunction with four-nucleon transfer reactions, have made it possible to establish the level densities for both the ground state and the 0+ excited state in 64Ni at zero spin. By comparing the level densities with the macroscopic-microscopic method, it was discovered that the ground state and the 0+ excited state in 64Ni exhibit distinct properties due to their different levels of pair alignment. Furthermore, the level densities in 64Ni agree with global trends, but exhibit a more rapid increase with energy than predicted by the macroscopic-microscopic method.

Our study examines how model performance variability affects parameter tuning for natural language processing tasks. We investigated the impact of different validation techniques on estimator variance and bias, using a range of NLP tasks and popular machine learning algorithms. Our key discovery is that the risk estimate produced during tuning exhibits significant unpredictability, leading to poorly informed decisions about the optimal number of models to train. We found that reducing the number of models used in k-fold cross-validation, especially with tenfold CV, fails to adequately estimate the model's expected performance. To put this issue into perspective, using tenfold CV to tune a model leads to an estimated performance that is one standard error away from the estimated performance obtained using the holdout method with the full training dataset. We propose using (J-1)k-fold cross-validation, leaving out one subset for evaluation, as a simple and effective strategy to reduce estimator variance and bias.

Deep neural networks have achieved superior performance in various knowledge-based tasks by applying knowledge learning. To enhance efficiency and effectiveness, knowledge learning methods are being developed with instructor-student architectures, where an student model acquires knowledge from an instructor model through training. These methods have significantly improved knowledge acquisition for the student model, allowing it to obtain comparable or even superior performance to the instructor model with less training data. As a result, instructor-student knowledge learning architecture has been widely adopted across multiple fields. This survey delves into the fundamentals of knowledge learning, before examining instructor-student knowledge learning architecture in depth. It also explores the existing literature on knowledge learning architecture, categorized by knowledge sources, optimization objectives, and circuit-oriented designs. Furthermore, the survey extracts and presents the knowledge acquisition analysis, transfer learning analysis, and robustness analysis of the student model. It also discusses the application of instructor-student knowledge learning architecture in deep neural networks.

We introduce a new efficient algorithm for the exact Maximum Probability Explanation (MPE) problem and constrained optimisation in graphical models by leveraging a novel brief function representation (BFR) (Theorem 1). By examining the model through a series of conceptual BFR layers, our method accurately determines the optimal nodes for sampling in just two steps. Our results show that by using BFR, we can significantly reduce the number of admissible values compared to the standard variable elimination method. Furthermore, our method enables seamless constrained optimisation by simply adding constraints to the BFR layers. Our algorithm's performance is particularly notable for models that feature loops of variables, achieving a notable improvement of 3 times in terms of admissible values when compared to variable elimination.

We investigated single-photon absorption using a cold strontium-88 gas within a cavity-enhanced spectroscopy setup, and have demonstrated the occurrence of photon recoil effects through momentum transfer during the absorption of a 128 terahertz photon. Due to the tiny size of the gas atoms relative to the wavelength of the light used, forward scattering occurs, resulting in the direction of light being altered. As a result, we observed light propagation changes, specifically the development of a conical structure and light scattering deep within the gas cloud. Furthermore, we determined the precise characteristics of this conical structure, comparing them to theoretical predictions.

The sudden loss of fluidity that occurs during shear thickening transitions poses a long-standing challenge for modeling and predicting fluid behavior. Researchers have observed that shear thickening transitions often follow a universal pattern of of "stick-slip" failures under steady shear stress. To better understand this phenomenon, a comprehensive analysis is performed on stress-strain data from lab and real-world experiments involving shear thickening materials. By applying a novel scaling approach that accounts for initial conditions, the authors reveal a universal law governing the failure process. This law is then used to demonstrate the equivalence of various shear thickening transition models and to predict the outcomes of subsequent shear thickening interactions. Moreover, the scaled approach is applied to a dataset from actual vehicle accidents involving shear thickening fluid (STF) used in critical applications.

Recently, a higher rank analogue known as the Racah algebra was found to be part of the $\mathfrak{sl}_n$ centralizer chain. By utilizing the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ basis expansion approach, the focus on the second centralizer $Z_2(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ reveals its isomorphic nature to the braid algebra $B_2$ and the Askey-Wilson algebra AW_2. Furthermore, the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of $Z_2(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be determined through a newly introduced composition-substitution method, resulting in the calculation of $|Z_2(\mathfrak{sl}_2):B_2| = 2$ and $|Z_2(\mathfrak{sl}_2):AW_2| = 4$.

An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the influence they have on retrieving all relevant information. The study's results show that a substantial number of the participants are unaware of potential biases in search algorithms and the possible strategies to prevent them from overlooking essential information. Notably, when considering the potential biases, officials had a 25 per cent drop in their success in identifying correct answers. Moreover, there was a notable disparity in how well they could find all the relevant information, with a 30 per cent drop in successful outcomes. Overall, the study's findings suggest that because of Web search personalisation, government officials may be losing sight of crucial information, leading to biased assessments that could have considerable consequences for the public.

We're proposing the concept for a muon collider that operates at the TeV level and can serve either as a standalone facility or be integrated into an existing complex with an Higgs factory. We're examining two main configurations for this collider: one with a geometric luminosity of 5 ab^-1 and two possible total particle energies of 2 TeV, with either 100 A^0 currents or 50 A^0 currents. We then outline various detection strategies and ideal particle signatures for three main categories of physics research: Higgs physics within the Standard Model, Higgs physics that deviates from the Standard Model, and beyond-the-Standard Model physics. We're also presenting design requirements and innovative ideas for the detector, as well as anticipated computational demands for various analyses and anticipated research outcomes.

A novel approach to T2-weighted 4D MRI with respiratory compensation and motion correction has been developed. Utilizing a spatially encoded respiratory acquisition technique, it provides consistent imaging volume filling and allows for efficient data acquisition, sorted and reconstructed through PSF-based reconstruction, which results in respiratory compensation and efficient reduction of motion-related artifacts. Furthermore, a sophisticated framework has been implemented to minimize long-term variations in motion patterns, specifically suitable for scanning periods exceeding several minutes. In a study involving ten healthy subjects, data was collected through both conventional and spatially encoded respiratory acquisition protocols, with comparable image quality according to a study.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has seen significant improvements, thanks to advances in computational power. However, the number of tests conducted at each time point is still relatively large, leading to a desire for more precise methods while maintaining efficient computation. We introduce an accurate paired-permutation testing approach using test statistics aligned with model structure, aiming to enhance the efficacy of computational resources. Evaluations across five languages demonstrate our method's effectiveness and various benefits, including reduced standard error and computation time. We also explore different test frequency effects on error rates. Our code is available at GitHub.

A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for the six primary shipping routes. Furthermore, instructions on combining and verifying datasets are provided using the knowledge of shipping industry specialists and former top executives. A descriptive analysis of previously unstudied market phenomena known as the "container crisis" is conducted with this data. Structural changes in the data variables are then identified to demonstrate how the shift to container shipping affected the market.

We define loom areas for a collection of edges crossing a circle, building on the concept of veering triangulations. These areas evolve over time, mirroring the changes in triangulations and are linked to the dynamics of the cross-ratio. Specifically, we show that the time derivative of the loom area at any time is equal to the absolute value of the derivative of the cross-ratio. Furthermore, loom areas achieve their minimum and maximum values at times when the cross-ratio has local extrema or changes abruptly.

Techniques such as sentiment analysis and stock price prediction rely heavily on
the interpretation of financial news. The use of traditional methods like support
vector machines and technical indicators has been common practice; however,
the emergence of deep learning models, specifically sentiment analysis using BERT
and generative adversarial training for prediction, has been less explored.
Our research involves using a combination of BERT and GAN to forecast stock
values. FinBERT, a custom model based on BERT, was created to analyze the
sentiment of financial news, which was then combined with a feature engine to
enrich the data. Subsequently, a GAN was developed to forecast stock values.
The model showed superior performance compared to traditional methods like ARIMA
and machine learning models, with an RMSE of 0.34 and a MAE of 0.20 for the
test dataset.

Our study delves into the capabilities of future $e^+e^-$ colliders with high energy outputs to detect beyond-Standard Model (BSM) Higgs interactions via the observation of double Higgs boson production. Leveraging accurate Effective Field Theory-based predictions, we assess the optimal operating energy and luminosity requirements for such a detector. Specifically, under assumed detector responses, we calculate the minimal observable double Higgs production signal above the background at different collider configurations. Our analysis reveals that an operating energy of 250-350 GeV is ideal to detect double Higgs production, and that the required luminosity should be in the range of 5-100 ab$^{-1}$. Furthermore, we outline the progress made in calculating double Higgs production cross-sections within the Standard Model and its extensions, including its interplay with QCD corrections, as well as the impact of kinematic distributions on detector sensitivity.

We demonstrate the existence of a well-posed initial-value problem for the Einstein evolution equations in a gravitationally accelerated frame of reference, allowing for the inclusion of a cosmological constant within the framework of general relativity.

We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical object moving through a layer of granular material at various speeds, particularly at the point where it starts to move, to better understand the complex dynamics involving the object and the surrounding material. Calculations showed that the object's forward speed has a significant impact on its starting speed, due to friction within the object itself, the surrounding material, and the object's length. Additionally, we found that the drag experienced by the object is affected by its orientation, with the drag being greater when it's moving sideways than when it's moving lengthwise. These findings held true regardless of the object's starting speed or the characteristics of the surrounding material.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered that triangular flow's dependence on centrality is influenced by anisotropic initial geometry, given that transverse momentum dependence is disregarded. However, once transverse momentum dependence is considered, we found that triangular flow's dependence on centrality is driven by the correlation between initial radial and angular anisotropic geometries, resulting in similar centrality dependencies for elliptical and triangular flows.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes such as flavour-changing neutral currents and radiative leptonic decays. These findings are based on data collected between 2010 and 2012, with a total integrated luminosity of 3.0 inverse femtobarn for 8 TeV proton-proton collisions. The results include updated measurements of the D0 and $\phi_K$ lifetimes, in addition to precise determinations of the CP-violating parameters in the $B^0_s \to J/psi(\mu\mu)$ and $B^0 \to J/psi(\mu\mu)$ systems of mesons. Furthermore, the ratio of branching fractions for $B_s \to \mu^+\mu^- $ to $B_d \to \mu^+\mu^- $ has been measured with unprecedented accuracy. Lastly, the ATLAS collaboration has observed the rare decay processes $B \to K^* \gamma$ and $B_s \to \phi \gamma$, and has also detected the flavour-changing neutral current process $B^0 \to \tau^+\tau^- $.

A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for partial differential equations is maintaining the underlying properties of the original solution through approximation. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including studying the implications of approximating the inverse of a matrix with a specific structure within the context of iterative solutions to linear systems. However, the introduction of preconditioned Krylov methods has presented a significant challenge, given the limited understanding of how the choice of the approximate inverse affects the structure of the solution when approximating the inverse of a matrix with a particular structure. This study aims to address this knowledge gap by examining the effects of different preconditioned Krylov methods on the preservation of the structure of the solution, specifically focusing on the behavior of the residual and the iterates within the methods, and demystifying the intricate patterns observed in figure 2.

We present a novel method for non-rigid registration that maps soft organ volumes to their corresponding surface data. This surface-volume registration is critical for accurate organ segmentation in pre-operative scenarios. Our approach leverages a data-driven biomechanical model that tracks the organ's deformable behavior based on past surgical data. This model enables us to perform registration even when the surface and volume data have significantly different dimensions. We evaluate our method on real data, comparing it to standard techniques and finding that it outperforms them according to multiple assessment metrics. Moreover, our method achieves satisfactory results on a separate, unrelated dataset. We also examine the impact of various parameters on the model's performance and discuss its limitations. This study was conducted within the scope of abdominal organ surgery.

We investigate the self-supervised metric learning approach for scene flow estimation, focusing on an problematic aspect where models trained on synthetic data with intentional errors perform similarly to those trained on real data without such distortions. We introduce a novel framework, Adversarial Metric Learning for Self-supervision (ALPS), that addresses this challenge by creating a competitive environment where models must surpass a threshold of accuracy on a test set with distorted data points. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ALPS by incorporating it into a self-supervised training regime, leading to a significant improvement in results when compared to traditional self-supervision methods. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhengyang0721/ALPS.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for initial setup and ongoing operation. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's effectiveness across real-world classification datasets.

Within the framework of the relativistic mean field model, using the Lagrangian density, the thermodynamic metrics of spin-polarized strange quark stars were investigated at finite temperature and in the presence of a strong magnetic field.

We have achieved substantial progress in addressing a significant aspect of Levene and Parson's 1972 conjecture regarding the relationship between certain numbers in cubic graphs. By constructing a specific subclass of cubic graphs, we meet a particular condition predicted by the conjecture. Furthermore, this subclass leads to insights that connect with a conjectured optimal lower bound on the number of Hamiltonian cycles in a cubic graph with a specified property, as well as with the need to modify a well-known conjecture related to edge-colourings.

This paper introduces a new method, called Timeloops, which automatically learns policies for system call filtering in containerized microservices. By blocking unnecessary system calls between containers, Timeloops prevents malicious container escape attacks and limits the attack surface. It achieves this by leveraging lightweight hooks in the Linux kernel and intelligent policy suggestions based on runtime observation. In contrast to static analysis and binary rewriting techniques, Timeloops takes a dynamic approach, allowing system calls to be freely enabled or disabled during execution. Through benchmarks, it is shown that Timeloops incurs minimal performance costs, ranging from 1.16% to 5.13% slow down in application response time. Additionally, it is demonstrated that Timeloops can effectively prevent container escape attacks and coexist with existing security solutions.

A previous study introduced a Bernoulli filter, which was efficient but problematic due to its uniform origin model. This research enhances the filter by using a non-uniform grid-based origin model, specifically tailoring the intensity function to match target characteristics. In addition, we've modified the algorithm to adapt sampling strategies dynamically in sensor management scenarios. Through numerical tests, we've demonstrated that the revised filter outperforms the original in tracking accuracy, while also offering substantial improvements in false alarms.

This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior decay term, specifically within the framework of a parabolic system of equations. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety and then deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a control region that enables the controllable null space within the framework of a strong sense.

The objective of a soccer player's action depends on the game's stage, its current state, and the player's position of authority. Research has been done on predicting the optimal action in a soccer game state, but it doesn't consider the game's critical stage. Moreover, there is limited understanding of the player's state of authority that is not tied to specific positions on the field. To address these limitations, we developed a novel approach by creating a continuous framework of state of authority and divided the game's stage into its critical and non-critical phases. We utilized deep reinforcement learning to train a policy network that predicts the optimal action in a soccer game state. To evaluate the model's performance in the game's non-critical phases, we used a simulator that met the NSOAR competition rules. Furthermore, we applied our model to the game's critical stages.

High-frequency seismic data analysis relies heavily on accurate modeling of seismic wave behavior within complex geological environments. The simulated data in synthetic seismic experiments should mimic real data characteristics as closely as possible to provide reliable and representative results. Our research involves developing an iterative approach to the time-domain ESI method by first applying an empirical semi-analytical F-K operator to the simulated data, followed by an empirical semi-analytical inverse F-K operator to the reconstructed data in each time-step. We tested and validated this method using real data from an air-gun source recording in a layered velocity structure, and observed significant improvements in the resolution of small targets buried within a large structure.

Research has shown that species competition can lead to both exclusive species survival or competitive exclusion through a tradeoff between colonization and competition abilities. Adding random fluctuations can result in species coexistence. This study uses the elector model to demonstrate how a colonization-competition tradeoff affects species competition dynamics, analyzing the impact of noise levels and initial species conditions on outcomes of interactions between two species. It is observed that larger differences in colonization and competition parameters at both the local and global levels can lead to coexistence, whereas a small parameter difference can lead to exclusive survival or competitive exclusion.

Our research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which allows for simultaneous energy harvesting and D2D communication within a cognitive radio network. This network, utilizing cognitive radio technology and D2D communication, features a cognition reflecting surface that aids an access point in making decisions regarding resource allocation. A novel algorithm was developed to maximize energy collection and data transmission rates while adhering to constraints related to D2D transmission power, D2D message exchange, and energy collection time. A reflecting surface optimization problem was formulated, and an iterative algorithm was proposed to solve it. It was demonstrated that the best strategy for the access point and the reflecting surface involves maximizing the D2D transmission rate and minimizing the energy collection time, with priorities given to users who can harvest and transmit energy and engage in D2D communication. Furthermore, our results showed that the proposed algorithm yields an optimal solution for a specific scenario.

The spatial resolution of single-point LDV systems is limited, yet these systems remain widely used for 2D velocity measurements. To overcome their limited spatial resolution, researchers have developed various techniques for calculating 2D velocity components from single-point measurements taken at offset locations. However, determining the optimal distance between the two probes is a significant challenge. Too great a distance results in the velocity components becoming undetermined, whereas a distance that is too small does not adequately account for the probe's limited spatial resolution. To address this issue, we calculated the cross-streamline probe distance as a fraction of the streamwise probe distance and tested it against experimental data featuring a turbulent airflow over a flat plate with a built-in obstacle. Our results showed that the 2D velocity reconstruction performs well when the cross-streamline probe distance is between 0.25 and 0.5 times the streamwise probe distance. Furthermore, we discovered that this range is sufficient to ensure that the velocity components are determinate and allows the 2D velocity reconstruction to be accurately calculated even in areas with complex flow dynamics.

The transmission electron microscope (TEM) has reached or is nearing the 1 Å resolution limit in imaging and 0.1 Å in structure determination due to advances in electron sources and aberration correction. To break this barrier, alternative methods for wavefront manipulation are being explored. We examine the potential of programmable phase plates as a means of wavefront modification within the TEM and investigate their capacity for compensating for the specimen-induced phase modification to achieve optimized imaging results. We propose and numerically verify a design for a programmable phase plate that can correct aberrations in the TEM. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, under certain conditions, a programmable phase plate capable of compensating for the specimen-induced phase modification can be as effective in image improvement as an aberration corrector in the TEM. We also explore the limitations and possible solutions for implementing such a design within the TEM.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in the context of the one-dimensional Klein-Gordon equation, coupled with an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of both types of stability, covering a range of anharmonic oscillator parameters and confirming or rejecting the commonly accepted condition of orbital stability within a specified range of $\delta>0$.

We derive new conclusions regarding the ideal factorization properties within extensions of the form K/Q, where Q is a number field and K is a subfield of Q that lies within a finite Galois extension of Q. These results include the idealistic proof of a key theorem from its computational counterpart and additionally imply the comprehensive property of partial field extensions.

To explore the production and detection of dark photons in the context of B meson decays, we concentrate on the decay channel $B\to K\gamma$ and calculate the number of dark photons that could be detected at the Belle II experiment via the B decay sequence $B\to K\gamma\to K\text{invisible}$. We calculate the expected number of signal events for the Belle II experiment operating at 50 ab$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity at the Kemel III energy range and find it to be 0.036$\pm$0.004 for a dark photon mass of 0.023eV and coupling strength of $10^{-3}$. We also consider other dark photon production channels in B meson decays such as $B\to K\text{invisible}\phi$ and $B_s\to \phi\text{invisible}$ and calculate the expected number of signal events for the Belle II experiment for these channels.

In our analysis of contextualized language models, we delived into the intricacies of their context-based workings, exploring their potential to identify changes to sentence semantics. Through contextualized vector representations, we demonstrated a conceptually straightforward approach that leverages contextual information, without needing advanced training protocols. To gauge their semantic alteration detection capabilities, we crafted a specially designed set of questions, extracting implicit sentence meanings from explicitly stated information. Our results showed that these models excel at uncovering embedded semantic details, detecting even the most subtle alterations to sentence meanings. Through our examination and tailored task engineering, we uncovered valuable insights into the contextualized workings of these models, coupled with novel detection methods that can be applied across diverse semantic alteration detection tasks.

We investigate the possibility of heavy quasars being surrounded by a disk that taps into their dark matter information, specifically focusing on the interplay between dark matter and a massive black hole through gravitational interaction. Based on calculations, we determine the expected spin characteristics of heavy quasars within a specific mass range (10^5 to 10^9 solar masses) for an assumed distribution of dark matter - in this case, ultralight axion-like particles with a mass range (10^-22 to 10^-17) Greese seconds. By analyzing a sample of 17 optically selected quasars with their spins estimated, we calculate the characteristics of ultralight bosons and compare our results to existing constraints and predicted limits from observations, including LIGO, QUMES, and FERMI-LYA.

A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei within the neural tissue layers, known as interkinetic nuclear migration. To gain insight into this process, researchers used high-speed imaging and advanced mathematical modeling to study interkinetic nuclear movement in zebrafish retinas. They found that the random movements of cell nuclei could be described as a diffusive process, and by measuring the distance they traveled, they estimated a key parameter called the nuclear movement coefficient. The results showed that this coefficient varies across different brain regions within the retina, with a notable correlation with the size of the granule layer neurons. Notably, the researchers were able to predict the distribution of nuclear movements using a random walk model and compared it to actual observations, finding they matched in the majority of cases. This research provides a quantitative understanding of interkinetic nuclear movement in zebrafish retinas.

Recently introduced codes called as Separation Changing Distortion Codes, Compressive Changing Distortion Codes and Progressive Changing Distortion Codes have shown superior performance in image denoising, deblocking, and color image demosaicing applications. We enhance these codes to further improve their decomposition accuracy and efficiency. For the newly introduced codes, we provide optimal reconstruction parameters that achieve the minimum distortion in each stage of decomposition. Furthermore, we prove that the newly introduced codes yield decay rates in the cosine series coefficients that converge rapidly, thereby providing a theoretical framework for their performance. We also analyze the decay rates in the basis coefficients for the compressive Changing Distortion Code and propose and evaluate variants of this code. Experimental results demonstrate the enhanced codes achieve superior performance in various applications.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies beyond two dimensions and provides a precise explanation for the characteristics of polar active liquids in the presence of randomly distributed obstacles. The model we've created includes a specific pattern of particle movement, driven by energy from their surroundings, as well as various responses to applied forces and torques. The dynamics of the model can be described by a set of pre-defined parameters that remain constant over time and are unaffected by spatial variations. Contrary to previous findings, our model reveals that polar order can persist indefinitely, even when the dimensionality is just slightly above two dimensions. Through our theoretical framework, we're able to demonstrate that the hydrodynamic theory contains multiple parameters that characterize the dynamics and have no equivalent in the random mangetization model. Furthermore, we found that the fluctuations of the model are resilient to compressions and the dimensions in which this resilience is ensured are higher than the lower threshold of two dimensions.

The rise in cloud computing has given rise to a significant increase in personal data being stored electronically. As a result, there is an growing need for techniques to extract vital information from these documents. Natural language processing is a key technology in this context, enabling institutions to meet their legal requirements for data privacy and security. An application in Indonesia called NIK extractor utilizes cloud computing and NLP to accurately identify and extract essential information from ID cards. This document includes details of the NIK extractor's development, starting with an analysis of its background, followed by discussions on the issues it addresses, its design, methodology, testing, and evaluation. A natural language processing approach is also presented, along with the extractor's source code, to facilitate replication.

Quantum mechanics involves measurable effects at the atomic level, but the study of these scales requires accounting for decoherence affecting long-range quantum connections. This research model assumes a form of environmental influence that degrades quantum correlations over a accessible time scale. We calculated the decay rate as well as stationary state properties through Jumps-MCMC simulations, verifying our results against available data.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a torque that causes their rotation velocities to increase over time. As a result, even when initially slow, these asteroids will eventually reach a state of high rotation velocity. To better understand this phenomenon, research focused on modeling three asteroids with known rotation velocities: 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro. By simulating their orbital histories, researchers determined that YORP is responsible for their current rotation velocities. Specifically, the results showed that YORP led to an increase in the rotation velocity of 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro of 0.0003, 0.01, and 0.006 degrees per day respectively, assuming direct YORP. Additionally, the analysis found that the YORP effect could be either direct or reversed in the case of Geographos, depending on the characteristics of its interior.

We show that any countable collection of surface homeomorphisms that map surfaces to a given surface within a specified distance, when viewed as a subset of the space of surface homeomorphisms at that distance, does not have a compact subset in the uniform convergence topology.

Finite automata can efficiently process infinite streams of data. To achieve this, a rational method is associated with each finite automaton through a formal construction. However, not all rational methods can be represented by finite automata, including those with infinite outputs or input dependencies. Recently, research has focused on categorizing and creating models of non-recognitive rational methods, specifically the type that includes data streams as inputs. In our work, we develop a framework for representing stream inputs and output mappings using recognizable rational methods, and demonstrate that any computable function that processes infinite data streams is equivalent to a rational function within this type of method. Furthermore, we provide a constructive proof that any computable function is approximable to any desired degree of precision.

A machine learning technique known as advanced autonomous exploration (AAE) is proposed to discover new, unseen stable states existing alongside other stable states in complex systems. Through a stochastic search approach, AAE identifies distinct, isolated reservoir states and maps them to a lower dimension, facilitating the detection of regions corresponding to existing attractors. By analyzing the dynamics of these regions, researchers can determine the dynamics of the system's attractors and identify boundaries between them. These boundaries are found to be stable even when noise is introduced, demonstrating the effectiveness of AAE in a noisy environment. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated by applying it to multiple complex systems including a noisy multistable system, a system with nonlinear dynamics, and a biological model, and it is compared to other machine learning models.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features, face processing, or agency. In the current study, we examine the animacy organization in VTC using functional connectivity and gradient maps. Our findings show that the connection between the anterior part of the lateral occipital complex (LOa) and VTC plays a significant role in determining the animacy hierarchy. Furthermore, our results demonstrate a connection between the fronto-parietal network and VTC that is associated with the human's agency perception in animated figures. When evaluating gradient maps based on face processing, we found a subregion within VTC that is associated with the perception of human faces. Notably, this relationship exists across cultures. Our approach also allows us to identify a subregion within VTC that is linked to the perception of animals with human-like characteristics. A comparison of our methods to previous studies on VTC is also presented. The approach used in this study provides a non-parametric approach to determining the spatial extent of animacy-related gradients within VTC. The findings of our study are consistent with a previous study by Aerts et al. (2019), which used a parametric approach to analyze the animacy hierarchy.

The study proves the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros or confirms the quantum unique ergodicity of GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms at a calculable pace, supported by the broader conclusion that Dirichlet L-function zeros exert a force pushing zeros from all other automorphic L-functions off the s=1 axis.

We introduced a new variant of quantum relational Hoare reasoning, which involves assigning values to variables that are represented as pairs of expectations. These expectations represent the possible values of variables in two programs being compared, where the order of the variables can be different. We created a set of rules for proving the validity of pre-post conditions in programs using relational Hoare reasoning, and demonstrated its equivalence to a simpler set of rules that does not involve pairs of expectations. We also showed that this approach is applicable to a wide range of programs by proving the soundness of a library of program components, and provided an example of using these components to prove the correctness of a program.

The severity of an epidemic is often exacerbated by a single individual whose highly contagious interaction results in a substantial increase in new cases. By incorporating super-spreader events into an existing contact-tracing model, our study demonstrates their significant potential to quickly multiply an otherwise contained epidemic into a full-blown crisis. Our findings indicate that in comparison to traditional models, the spread of an epidemic can be described as exponential rather than exponential with eventual decline.

Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with the set of bounded linear operators acting on X, referred to as L(B,X). We derive an important property regarding the existence of a basis in the complex algebra A(L,B,X). Specifically, for the algebra A to have a basis, it must include at least three distinct operators within the set L(B,X). This necessary condition for a basis in A(L,B,X) can be demonstrated via two distinct proofs.

The accuracy of solar vector magnetometry depends on the reliability of magnetic inclination and azimuth measurements from spectroscopic data, which can be influenced by broadening models and plasma conditions. Studies have shown that using actual observed values of $D_3$ and $f$ broadening instead of their average values removes the systematic bias in magnetic inclination and azimuth measurements. However, the accuracy of these observed values must be verified to ensure they are unbiased. We show that using the observed values of $D_3$ and $f$ broadening without consideration for their properties and measurement methods may lead to biased magnetometry data. Specifically, we find the expected bias in magnetometry data when observed values are used, expressed in terms of the scatter of $D_3$ and $f$ broadening and the measurement errors of inclination and azimuth. We then discuss the requirements for the observed values to be unbiased, which includes the precision of $D_3$ and $f$ broadening and the measurement errors of inclination and azimuth. Furthermore, we propose a more precise formulation of the relationship between $D_3$ and $f$ broadening that allows for the characterization of deviations from a single-scattering model, which may also account for the complex dynamics of plasma turbulence.

A sign issue arises in Monte Carlo methods within many-electron simulations due to the inaccuracy of reweighting factors, posing a significant challenge for time-dependent and finite-temperature calculations using neural network-based autoregressive Hamiltonians. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel framework based on complex-valued neural networks that eliminates the need for reweighting factors by directly producing correct signs. This model is derived from a standard neural network through a simple complex transformation, allowing the use of existing training protocols. Furthermore, we demonstrate that complex networks offering multiple output options can achieve accurate results without reweighting by selecting the correct sign through a loss function, thereby providing a linear increase in computational costs.

Given any non-erasing free monoid homomorphism and integer $n \geq 1$, it is demonstrated that the resulting composite map increases topological entropy by a factor of at most $n$. Furthermore, with respect to a specific type of homomorphisms associated with the basis change of free groups, it is shown that the resulting complexity function achieves a growth rate of at most $n$ for the $n$th composition iteration.

By leveraging previously collected data, models can transfer knowledge across tasks through generalization. However, when tasks are dissimilar, a well-established model may produce misleading information due to the influence of irrelevant data, thereby compromising performance. We address the challenge of unsupervised cross-task generalization on heterogeneous datasets, distilling knowledge from a diverse set of examples without labeling, and demonstrating the efficacy of our approach on multiple datasets through rigorous experimentation. We develop a retrieber and encoder model that selectively incorporates relevant information from the dataset, adapting to new tasks without supervision. Through our experiments, we show that this approach yields superior results for both homogeneous and heterogeneous task sets, surpassing benchmarks by significant margins.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the context of differential privacy is challenging due to the restricted sample size that is typical in private machine learning. Additionally, the need to account for noise makes the relationship between hyperparameters and model performance uncertain. These issues are compounded by the difficulty of performing grid searches across hyperparameters in private learning, which is further limited by the already scarce sample size. We address these challenges by developing an efficient hyperparameter optimization framework that leverages the insights gained from public learning, combined with an accelerated Bayesian optimization technique, allows for the selection of optimal hyperparameters for over 10% more data, than is typically available in private learning. Our proposed method Leans towards models with lower privacy levels and thus prevents waste of more precious private data. Our method is evaluated using a dataset with a relatively large sample size (2400 samples) for tasks like MNIST, that typically require much larger datasets.

In this formalism, we examine the fundamental properties of boolean functions that satisfy a specific symmetry property related to an involution, particularly focusing on even-parity functions. Through the use of boolean algebra and properties of the involution operation, we establish proofs for a set of boolean functions that satisfy this symmetry, thereby demonstrating their incompatibility with the properties of switching functions. Additionally, we identify patterns that these compatible functions must adhere to.

We utilized two separate approaches to model the abundance patterns of 53,100 stars in the Milky Way disk, focusing on chemical elements beyond iron. With one method, we applied machine learning, specifically an artificial neural network, while the other involved fitting linear equations. Both approaches yielded consistent results and were compared to a known model of the galaxy's evolution. By analyzing residuals, we identified variations in abundance patterns across different regions of the galaxy, specifically in the outer bulge and the solar neighborhood. These patterns revealed how elements are created and destroyed in the galaxy's center and its outer regions, and how the galaxy's evolution affects the distribution of elements over time.

The rapid dissemination of online rumors poses a significant threat to community safety, especially in times of crisis. To combat this issue, it is essential to understand the parameters that drive the spread of rumors. Our study leverages real-world data from the Sina Weibo platform to analyze the dynamics of rumor propagation during the COVID-19 pandemic. By developing a mathematical framework based on the spread method and influence of rumors, our findings reveal that the most influential users driving the propagation of rumors often occupy the periphery of social networks. Moreover, our data indicates that only a small portion of rumors spread quickly, with most being confined to a narrow local community. Our research also shows that the removal of false information has a more substantial impact on slowing its dissemination than the addition of new influential users. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the remaining period of a rumor's lifecycle is significantly shorter than its initial propagation phase.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed sample needs to be distinguished from foreground Galactic planetary nebulae. We developed a distinct code using machine learning and astrometric constraints to separate extragalactic planetary nebulae. The code was applied to the extensive database from the Fornax3D survey, resulting in an estimated 11,567 planetary nebulae associated with galaxies within the Fornax cluster. By correlating planetary nebulae with stars in the same line-of-sight, we obtained reliable distance measurements to galaxies in the Fornax cluster with an average error of 1.3%. Additionally, a significant mismatch was found between the positions and brightness levels of planetary nebulae in two major galaxy subgroups within the Fornax cluster, likely caused by differences in star formation histories.

In areas like network analytics, finance, and biomedical research, programs that process data streams consistently excel over their one-time applications. These programs generally require efficient implementations that are both highly effective and easy to program. Despite the growing demand for efficient stream programs, there is limited guidance on how to optimize stream declarations and implementations effectively. In response, we developed an evaluation framework called StreamDeclEval that assessments of stream declarations' impact on data streams are scarce. Following a thorough examination of various stream declarations' effects, we found notable improvements in program efficiency by simply rearranging the program structure with little impact from declarations. Consequently, we discovered that the best implementation, in terms of overall performance, is not necessarily the most complex one. As a result, we recommend programs maintain lightweight declarations while favoring streamlined program structures. Furthermore, we found that programs preferably process current data over historical data, preferably with delayed windows.

We establish a semi-metric characterization of timelike Bertrand curves in a semi-metric space, expanding on the metric-based findings of Ghomi and the first author. Additionally, we provide a formula for the semi-metric derivative of these curves, which can be further utilized to define a differential operator acting on the semi-metric space.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a critical parameter that significantly affects the performance and safety of trained models. As a result, it is essential to conduct thorough testing and validation to ensure the chosen loss function is optimal. Nonetheless, the existing literature largely overlooks the examination of loss functions that are commonly employed without modification, namely the default loss functions provided by deep learning libraries. This study investigates the consequences of using the categorical cross-entropy loss function with approximate softmax reversals, an intriguing phenomenon observed during training with data augmentation. We discovered that using this loss function leads to improved performance, exceeding that of the standard loss function by approximately 1% in our experiments. We further analyze this finding by considering the relationship between loss function variation and k-NN similarity, ultimately demonstrating the scalability of our observation to diverse datasets.

This research aims to advance the simulation capabilities of polymers undergoing strain-induced crystallization, as well as their mechanical and thermal properties, by drawing on experimental data and imaging techniques. The study focuses on a specific type of polymer called polyethylene, but the proposed methods and analysis can be applied to other materials and scenarios. To accurately depict the onset and growth of crystals, a comprehensive analysis was conducted using high-speed imaging and advanced testing equipment. This analysis helped identify critical parameters influencing crystal formation, including temperature, slip rates, and shear rates. The results were used to establish equations describing the development of crystals and associated material properties. Furthermore, the study involved assessing the proposed methods' validity and reliability through comparisons of simulated and actual results.

Within the framework of a $d$-wave nematic superconductor, we calculated the magnetic response of fermion couples to a weak external magnetic field. Our results show that Pauli paramagnetic response is evident for triplet couples, whereas singlet couples exhibit diamagnetic behavior. Moreover, the magnitude of the paramagnetic response was found to be directly proportional to the concentration of triplet couples. A second-order magnetic susceptibility coefficient was derived and analyzed in the limit of low concentrations of triplet couples. In this limit, the coefficient's sign and value were determined to be negative and inversely related to the concentration of triplet couples. Notably, the paramagnetic response can be experimentally detected through measurement of the specific heat discrete peak shift in the external magnetic field.

In this work, we examine the performance of coherent differential CPM detection methods, focusing on their delay resistance properties. We develop an analytical framework to assess delay resistance, drawing on cyclostationary theory. Our analysis reveals that the delay resistance of these detection methods can be evaluated via the cyclostationarity of their autocorrelation functions. We then apply this framework to investigate the delay resistance of conventional detection schemes based on differential CPM signals, specifically cycloplethysmographic detection, phase-shift keying detection, and frequency-shift keying detection. We derive new analytical criteria for these detection methods' delay resistance performance. Our study shows that the suitability of these detection methods is determined by their autocorrelation function's periodic correlation properties. We further propose a delay resistance performance metric, incorporating the maximum periodic correlation coefficient, to facilitate method comparison and selection. To validate our analysis, we generate simulation data based on our models and analyze the performance of the detection methods employed. Our findings indicate that the best detection method should balance its computational complexity and delay resistance performance.

A previous study introduced the concept of vacuum compressibility in quantum spacetime, inversely related to the change in logarithmic volume due to a change in energy density. It was demonstrated that this compressibility serves as a metric for quantifying the complexity of spacetime models. Here, the compressibility metric is applied to static spacetime scenarios resulting from the union of isolated black holes and cosmological spaces of the type $Schwartzschild$ and $Kerr$. Furthermore, the study of complex sources such as black holes with scalar fields and $F$-branes rolling down their potential energy landscapes is explored. Additionally, the focus is on complex sources in the form of non-local, thermofield quantum chaos within $CFT_2$ dual spaces. Here, the relationship between the Lyre-Selby entropy and the compressibility metric is examined, along with the effects of shifting the conformal coupling or the central charge.

Our investigation into if-then logic revealed a complex landscape that lacks a linear narrative, and we believe this complexity holds the key to understanding the intricate relationship between rules and machine intelligence. In response, we've created ATOMIC, a comprehensive atlas that maps out the intricate pathways through machine intelligence using if-then logic. This atlas is guided by a set of principles that prioritize the interconnections between concepts and rules, rather than focusing solely on individual components. At the heart of ATOMIC lies a multi-dimensional map that represents the intellect's response to varying scenarios, and we believe this atlas offers a novel perspective on the internal workings of machine intelligence.

Our extension, NISQ-HHL, is a hybrid method that combines the HHL algorithm with investments in the quantum portfolio, aiming to optimize performance on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum devices. By reconfiguring the HHL algorithm's components, NISQ-HHL leverages the strengths of various quantum circuits to achieve the highest metadata efficiency and the lowest variance in the simulated phase estimation measurements. Compared to the original HHL algorithm, our results show that NISQ-HHL offers significant improvements, with a 324-fold decrease in metadata usage and a 25-fold decrease in the estimated execution time, using the Qiskit Aer Simulator on a quantum device with 64 logical qubits.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and improve their ability to generalize, we propose a novel multi-modal training method that combines text and speech inputs with a controlled feedback mechanism. In this approach, a decoder with a left-to-right and right-to-left configuration is employed to encode both the speech and text features, using the forward output to encode the speech and the backward output to encode the text. The encoded features are then fused and passed through a linear layer to produce the logit. We control the feedback by assigning a greater weight to the forward output when encoding the text and the backward output when encoding the speech. Experimental results on the Librispeech corpus reveal a 6.15% reduction in word error rate (WER) for the 5k test set and a 5.13% reduction in WER for the 10k test set when using the proposed method without an additional 300h background noise corpus. When using this corpus, the proposed method achieves a 9.16% reduction in WER for the 5k test set and a 7.33% reduction in WER for the 10k test set.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly selected uniform parking distribution of a given size, focusing on the asymptotic properties of the first n positions in the sequence. To accomplish this, we establish a combinatorial interpretation of the cumulative probability distribution, and further analysis via generating functions reveals an important connection to the growth rate of parking sequences. Additionally, we establish that the number of leading positions with a given property grows in proportion to n, with specific results provided for conditions involving the distance from the beginning, sum of values, and major index. A related examination is conducted on the subset of parking sequences with specified values in the initial positions.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. To further understand the behavior of these nanowires, measurements of dc conduction through NbN nanowire arrays, as well as individual nanowires, as a function of gate voltage were conducted. The results show that in arrays, a threshold voltage emerges that decreases with an applied negative gate voltage, consistent with previous findings. However, for individual nanowires within Joshi et al.'s study, the threshold voltage cannot be determined reliably. A model incorporating the energy of a single quantum phase slip and Coulomb blockade blocking can explain the observed effects. Consequently, the notion of coherent quantum phase slips must be reconsidered, and the term quantum phase slip should be used to describe the occurrence of single quantum phase slips within an array.

Our proposed approach leverages a dual neural network structure to accurately predict video data with a 100-degree field of view from a 40-degree field of view. The underlying assumption is that the camera's field of view is limited to 40 degrees. By employing two separate neural networks, one for the front half of the viewing sphere and one for the back half, we enable the model to effectively utilize the limited front-view perspective. Our key contribution is utilizing the predicted front-view video frame to forecast the back-half of the viewing sphere, which is then transformed into the original coordinate system to obtain the predicted video frame in the original perspective. The model's efficacy is reflected in its ability to correctly predict video data with a 100-degree field of view for various tasks, including classification, segmentation, and detection, while also surpassing the performance of alternative methods.

In this research, we demonstrated the inter-plate coupling effect using NeAr autoionizing states as an example. By adjusting the spacing between two silver plates, we modified the energy difference between two singly ionized state levels, specifically the fine structure within the 3s$\sigma$ electron-aeration state, and observed a change in their spectral features. Specifically, as the plates' distance was decreased below a certain point, we noticed a shift in the energy spectrum, which took on a characteristic 2D roton behavior. All experiments were carried out within a vacuum environment, with the plates' surfaces kept clean to minimize scattering off surface atoms.

Within the Quark Model, we conduct an in-depth analysis of $\Omega^{-}$ baryon properties, evaluating the masses and form factors of this exotic particle. We utilize three methods to calculate mass predictions: the $^3P_2$-only approach, the 10-parameter fit, and the 12-parameter fit, with results compared to empirical data from the Particle Data Group. We also calculate magnetic and electric form factors at various momentum transfers, comparing our findings to output from a constituent quark model and experimental data from Jefferson Lab.

A well-mixed model assumes that individuals within a group are uniformly mixed and exposed to the same risk factors. Research aims to compare and contrast outcomes from a closed model to those observed in a real-world setting, specifically on an urban bus. By varying the speed of the bus, researchers examined how density and slow movement affect the spread of an airborne pathogen. They discovered that even at high speeds, the transmission rate remained linked to the probability of a single encounter between an infected and uninfected individual. Furthermore, they found that the critical distance between passengers exerting influence on each other could be estimated as three meters.

The spin-orbit proximity effect is a key feature that arises from the interaction between a material and a nearby source of spin-orbit coupling. As a result, the electronic properties of the original material can be modified, leading to the emergence of unique properties such as the spin-orbit coupling in graphene. In the case of ferromagnetic multilayers, accurate analysis requires consideration of the complex interplay between spin-orbit coupling, magnetic anisotropy, and interface interaction. A theoretical model is presented, incorporating the effects of spin-orbit coupling, magnetic anisotropy, and interface interaction on Co layers within a Bi/Co multilayer. According to the model, the magnitude of the spin-orbit coupling in the Co layers depends on the strength of the interface interaction. A critical interface interaction threshold is identified, above which the spin-orbit coupling in the Co layers suddenly increases, leading to the transformation of the magnetic anisotropy from uniaxial to biaxial behavior. These findings are supported by experimental data from Bi/Co multilayers, demonstrating that the spin-orbit coupling in the Co layers can be controlled through the strength of the interface interaction.

This paper provides the framework for the ground state wave function within the context of the time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space, with the ground state energy calculated for a generalized Mie-type potential that includes fractional derivatives.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimization problem that can be resolved via an iterative gradient descent method.
