Ten years ago, at the inaugural PxTP workshop, veriT's input format was introduced, a simple text-based format for SAT and SOLvers. Since then, veriT has evolved significantly, incorporating features from SMT-LIB and supporting multiple theories. However, its underlying structure has remained consistent, separating assertions, assumptions, and additional facts using specialized constructs. In contrast, SMT-LIB's standard input format combines assumptions and assertions within a single list of formulas. The veriT solver now fully adopts this standard, eliminating the distinct construct for assertions. This change aligns veriT with other solvers, facilitating its use within integrated proof systems.

As the number of mobile devices participating in FL increases, the gradient collection time also rises, leading to a delay that hampers high-speed model updates. Scheduled FL algorithms address this issue by tying update and aggregation schedules to model update speeds and communication latencies, yet they overlook the possibility of differing gradient collection times. We present the Async Buffered FL algorithm, which effectively handles disparate delay patterns by separating users into distinct groups based on their communication latencies and corresponding gradient update schedules. The algorithm aggregates models asynchronously, using a shared storage space, it ensures robustness against delayed or disconnected users. Furthermore, we prove that, under certain conditions, the algorithm yields models that converge at a similar rate as scheduled FL algorithms. To illustrate the benefits of this algorithm, we conduct experiments on MNIST and EMR datasets with delayed users and show that it outperforms scheduled FL algorithms by reducing average model update latency by up to 7 times.

Recently, end-to-end neural network-based speech recognition systems have achieved significant improvements, however, these systems demand large amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across language barriers, such as using a model trained on English to recognize Spanish. Our research builds upon existing methods by utilizing multiple target languages in a single training session, a technique we call multi-target training. Furthermore, we divide the task into finer sub-tasks by a process called cascade connection, which enables the handling of more challenging languages in the training process. We train and test these models on a dataset consisting of 60 languages, including many low-resource languages, with results showing they can effectively recognize multiple languages with comparable efficiency to models trained on a single language.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes significant challenges in guiding marine robots by utilizing underwater sensors and radio frequency signals. Our model leverages spatial and temporal correlations in data to create efficient guidance. By forming a joint model of value functions and observations, we developed a Gaussian Process TD learning algorithm that provides a theoretical guarantee for policy improvement. Our methodology also incorporates multiple data sources and facilitates the incorporation of prior knowledge. Our research delivers several key advancements: (1) we established the opportunity for TD learning in the presence of abundant data with intrinsic variability; (2) we created a Gaussian Process TD learning method with a guaranteed positive policy improvement; and (3) we established the opportunity for sparse models in the presence of limited data with intrinsic variability. Our research delivers several key technological advancements: (1) we established the possibility of using TD learning when there is abundant data with intrinsic variability; (2) we created a Gaussian Process TD learning method with a proven advantage; and (3) we created a sparse model that can be used when there is little data with intrinsic variability.

We employ a comprehensive anisotropic dark fluid model to examine the structure and stability of compact stellar objects, leveraging the anisotropic dark fluid's pressure and energy density differences to drive relativistic hydrodynamic equations. By applying the anisotropic dark fluid model within the context of General Relativity, we derive a set of modified Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations, from which we determine the metric potential, mass function, and binding energy. Furthermore, we establish conditions for stability through the second-order covariant conservation equation, specifically by taking the trace and anisotropic component. By numerically solving these equations, we obtain mappings for objects across various mass ranges and density ratios. Notably, we find that objects in the anisotropic category, when compared to their isotropic counterparts, exhibit greater mass ranges and more substantial density ratios.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based grammatical error correction models focus primarily on combining multi-domain data. However, combining data from diverse sources can sometimes lead to style contamination and negatively impact performance. In contrast, few-shot domain transfer approaches show promise, leveraging the idea that similar linguistic structures across domains enable efficient adaptation. We take this a step further by integrating data from just two domains in our method, domain selection in the meta-test phase. Specifically, we select the domain where new sentences are drawn from, based on grammatical error patterns, without prior knowledge. Our proposed approach, few-shot domain selection GEC, leverages experience to inform efficient adaptation in the meta-test phase. We evaluate this approach on the NUS GEC at NLP Upstream Challenge 2020, achieving the highest results among entry-level models on both test sets.

The problem of allocating discrete goods to self-interested agents with incomplete information has been well-examined in mathematics and computer science. In the context of indivisible goods, where agents can reject items, allocating items via strategy-proof mechanisms is a well-stated goal, achieving pure Nash equilibria being a specific subgoal. Our study identifies a broad class of mechanisms, for which we can guarantee the existence of a pure Nash equilibria in which all agents are satisfied, or for which we can determine the conditions under which this equilibrium exists. Furthermore, we connect this condition to fair allocation criteria like envy-free allocation.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal bright arms and a massive, narrow H-alpha band indicating rapid star formation. This galaxy exhibits a distinctive lack of large-scale H I gas, with a significant discrepancy between its optical and radio luminosity. High-resolution H I observations reveal a vast, irregular H I disk surrounding the galaxy, composed of multiple, scattered H I clouds. These clouds are loosely bound to UGC 8839 and originate from a collision with a nearby galaxy, likely NNGC 2903. The extensive H I cloud complex also includes a smaller H I stream flowing towards the Milky Way. UGC 8839's minimal stellar mass and the disconnection between its optical and radio luminosity suggest it's experiencing a prolonged period without significant star formation, exacerbated by a low gas supply. The vast H I disk around this galaxy offers valuable insights into the interplay between star formation, gas loss, and galaxy interactions.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of pion currents was conducted, examining both standard and Symanzik-improved gauge and fermion actions. Our study evaluated the spectral functions of various current combinations, comparing them to theoretical expectations based on chiral symmetry breaking and quark and antiquark properties. Our results showed that only currents composed of the same field type (e.g., $\bar{d}d$ versus $\bar{u}u$ or $\bar{d}u$ versus $\bar{u}\bar{d}$) exhibit distinct spectral structures, forming complex conjugate pairs. Furthermore, we determined the average mass of these structures and found it consistent with previous lattice studies, using sum rules of spectral functions.

Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution is closely tied to understanding how
mass accretion varies during this period, a topic that remains somewhat
enigmatic due to the complexities surrounding its measurement. To address this
challenge, an analysis was performed on the monochromatic mass-accretion rate
$\lambda$ using data from the $K2$ telescope for a sample of 15 young stars
with masses between 0.5 and 3.5 solar masses, spanning the 5 to 10 million
year age range. For most of these stars, measurements were found for multiple
years, allowing researchers to study their mass-accretion patterns over time.
A key observation from the data concerns the variable accretion patterns
exhibited by the sample stars, which display both persistent and transient
patterns of accretion. Further analysis of these variables revealed a
characteristic timescale of 0.25 to 0.5 solar masses for the stars with
masses between 0.5 to 3.5 solar masses, a finding that is in line with prior
research based on data from the $Spitzer$ telescope but over a longer
observation period. A notable exception among the sample stars is XX Cha,
which exhibits unusual and unusual patterns of accretion even when compared
to its peers that are of the same spectral type. A key outcome of this research
concerns the calculation of a new parameter called the accretion rate ratio

For multiple agents learning in a dynamic environment, offline multi-agent reinforcement learning is crucial. When interacting, agents can significantly impact the learning process through their actions affecting the reward function. This issue is addressed by proposing the Learning From Good Paths (LFGP) framework, focused on action policies rather than value functions. LFGP extracts high-quality action paths from historical data and prioritizes learning from them. A key aspect is the introduction of a module that aggressively explores the space of action policies. As a result, the model adapts around the most effective action paths, expanding on them to prevent stagnation. By incorporating both value-based and policy-based methods, the framework leverages the strengths of both approaches. Theoretical and practical insights into the benefits of the LFGP framework are provided, along with empirical results demonstrating its superiority over comparative methods.

We developed a novel approach for aligning MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, to compare with conventional template-based registration methods. Our dataset consists of 50 2D images and 10 3D images from two prostate patients, with known gold standard transformations. We evaluated our method, along with DNCTreg and GMM, on these datasets and recorded the results. Our findings indicate the proposed technique yields the lowest mean absolute error in 2D and 3D alignments, outperforming the compared methods.

A key distinction between classical and quantum nonlocality lies in the absence of a direct connection between monarchical correlations and the entanglement of individual particles. Our research focuses on single-particle entanglement in a bipartite scenario and explores its relationship with the classical nonlocal phenomenon known as steering. To achieve this, we analyze the conditions under which the unentangled outcome of a measurement on one particle affects the state of the other particle upon measurement on the first particle. Our study demonstrates that single-particle entanglement is a necessary condition for effects related to steering and provides a crucial insight into its own nature. Furthermore, we demonstrate that single-particle entanglement can result in effects related to steering even in scenarios where the particles are spatially separated in multiple dimensions.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence, smart transportation systems, and wireless communication technologies has led to a surge in data generation within the Internet of Vehicles (IoV). As a result, there has been growing interest in conducting machine learning tasks on IoV data, such as training models for secure, energy-efficient, and effective applications. However, the lack of a centralized infrastructure in IoV makes traditional machine learning approaches problematic. The advent of Federated Learning (FL) has provided a suitable alternative for handling IoV data, enabling the development of innovative technologies like secure, energy-efficient, and smart traffic management systems. FL allows multiple remote end-systems to collaborate in model training without exchanging sensitive data. The technique has shown significant potential in various IoV applications, including those related to cybersecurity, vehicular social networks, smart traffic management, drone-flown data collection, and autonomous vehicles. Despite the promising results, FL faces several challenges, notably related to data heterogeneity, participant trust, model security, and the complexity of hyperparameter tuning. To address these challenges, researchers have proposed various FL frameworks, including some that integrate FL with blockchain technology. The benefits of such integrated frameworks include enhanced security, credibility, and compliance with regulations like GDPR and HIPAA. The proposed frameworks often combine the strengths of both technologies while addressing drawbacks such as the computational costs and data homogeneity issues associated with FL. V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly declined in brightness within a week following its explosion, exhibited unusual behavior in the infrared spectrum throughout its decline.  V392 Persei's spectrum during this period was highly active, showing strong molecular aluminum oxides for an extended period, until its disappearance around 700 days after the explosion.  In addition to its pre-nova and post-nova spectra, the team detected a weak stellar component throughout its observations, indicating that the white dwarf in V392 Persei has not significantly changed since its initial observation in 2009.  The team also discovered a gamma-ray eruption 13 years prior to its known nova explosion, a time frame never before observed for a nova explosion.  The pre-nova and post-nova spectra of V392 Persei resemble those of the well-studied nova eruption V2499 Cygni, but with a notable difference in their infrared spectra decline rates.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to create codebooks and reduce feedback information. Unlike traditional approaches that use eigenvectors based on eigenvalue decomposition, this method involves generating codebooks from GMMs, which are trained in advance. Following testing in a simulated scenario, the proposed feedback scheme showed a 0.4-bit/s/Hz reduction in feedback information, while maintaining a 0.02-dB decline in average throughput. Additionally, performance was analyzed under channel estimation errors and noise, resulting in a 0.6-dB decline in throughput, which however improved to 0.02 dB in a more realistic simulation.

A type of sturdy nonequilibrium surface current has been identified that operates in three-dimensional Hofstadter models, even in their ground state. These currents, resistant to disruption, flourish along certain rugged interfaces and are driven by torsional magnetic fields. A key aspect of their functionality is their capacity to safeguard area-law behavior in nonequilibrium situations, most notably in protecting quantum annealers from faulty couplings. These findings are demonstrated through numerical simulations of a cubic lattice, and the principles are further illustrated using a simplified ribbon Hofstadter model.

Einstein's general relativity is contrasted with alternative gravity theories by measuring the mass change of rotating supermassive black holes. Using the Spectroscopic Survey of the SDSS-IV Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey, we calculated the spin of 69 stellar mass black holes with masses between 5 and 15 solar masses based on their stars' companions in binary systems. The method involved converting observed velocities into a standard frame, accounting for stars' movements. We determined the masses, radii, and luminosities of the stars, selecting main sequence stars with luminosities between one and five solar luminosities. The spin of the black holes was calculated using the relativistic Boltzmann distribution, with a tolerance of 0.1 due to measurement errors. The mass change to error ratio ranged from 10 to the power of negative 6 to 10 to the power of negative 5 for all but the most slowly spinning black holes, with an overall limit on mass change ratio of less than 0.001 for solar mass black holes. This limit holds for any density distribution of the black holes and is more restrictive than previous limits based on luminosity and X-ray data combined.

We examine the likelihood of low-mass black holes formed in the early universe through the merger of the first stars and their remnant dark matter, specifically within nuclear star clusters at the hearts of giant galaxies. Using a variety of theoretical approaches, including an analytical model and a numerical simulation of a galaxy with dwarf galaxies merging, we calculate the rate of such black holes formed in the early universe. Assuming these black holes are then found in the centers of giant galaxies, we estimate their merger rates with other black holes or neutron stars. Specifically, we predict the rates of GW150914-like events and GW170817-like binary neutron star events within the Milky Way and other similar galaxies.

In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to develop an efficient algorithm for finding optimal solutions for various system security constraints. We also investigate several suboptimal power allocation methods for multi-user relay systems with restricted channel state information. Through simulation results, we validate the efficacy of our proposed optimal algorithm and explore various non-idealized power allocation methods.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One key factor limiting the use of text-based games in challenging tasks is their slow speed, topping out at around 100 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three diverse text-based game environments, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over 1 million actions per second, making it vastly more efficient than its predecessors.
Furthermore, we demonstrate the substantial benefits of using TextWorldExpress in training artificial intelligence models, showing that our expression yields significantly better performance in narrow searches and problem-solving within text-based games.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various tasks including video identification. However, implementing these models on mobile devices is challenging due to their computational intensity and memory requirements. To overcome these limitations, we propose an algorithm and hardware co-design method that integrates a novel LSTM structure and a corresponding hardware accelerator. In the proposed LSTM model, each module's output is directly projected onto the output dimension, significantly reducing the storage needs without affecting performance. In the hardware accelerator, we designed a LSTM core with a hierarchical structure, featuring multiple small banks of storage that minimize data transfers and an efficient input/output path with a projection matrix multiplier. The proposed design was tested on a mobile application for video identification using the Hierarchical Tucker Tensor Decomposition method. Compared to a software implementation on an ARM Cortex-A53, the proposed hardware accelerator on an ASIC reduced computation time by 92 times and memory requirements by 98%.

In a theory with a well-defined stress-energy tensor within a CFT framework, the energy-momentum tensor of any operator is directly related to its two-point function. This relationship leads to the expectation that the energy-momentum tensor of a BPS operator in a d=4 SCFT will have a non-negative definite 4x4 stress-energy tensor symmetry matrix component. We have observed this expected behavior in a multitude of examples, spanning across various types of operators including chiral ring members, SYM coupled to certain types of vector and scalar fields, as well as certain BPS operators within the 3d and 5d SCFT spectra. Building upon these observations, we have formulated two conjectures regarding the positive definiteness of specific 4x4 matrices. When examining the energy-momentum tensor of a single operator within a 4d SCFT setup, we found that only one of the two matrices in question is always positively definite. In contrast, when considering the energy-momentum tensors of pairs of operators in 4d SCFT, we found that the combination of their sum is positively definite in all cases studied. This finding is in line with the expected outcome based on general principles of the AdS/BCFT framework. Moreover, we have also established the expected relationship in 3d and 5d SCFT settings.

Given any prime number p and suitable integers k and l, we establish the relationship between a ring's F-regular properties and the behavior of its tight Hilbert function, specifically within local rings containing a fraction field of rank one. This connection is particularly evident when examining the relationship between a ring's F-regularity and the condition that a specific power of its maximal ideal is completely reducible. Furthermore, this relationship can be seen as a natural extension of a result initially established by Huneke and Le, connecting a ring's F-regular properties with its depth and dimension within local rings of dimension two.

An important aspect of public policy involves providing auxiliary services such as vaccinations, online education, and mental health support. However, the demand for these services exceeds available supply, leading to significant waitlists. To effectively address this issue, it is crucial to consider the underlying dynamics of service demand and supply. By constructing a dynamic model that takes into account waitlists, quality of care, worker mobility, and COVID-19 patient flow, our study aims to provide a framework for policymakers to make data-driven decisions. A key feature of our model is the incorporation of optimal auxiliary service production levels that take into account worker training costs, a pay-for-performance scheme, and staffing constraints. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that introducing such an optimal production level can improve patient flow, reduce waitlists, and increase productivity. A numerical example illustrates the model's applicability in a realistic healthcare setting.

We investigate the properties of polynomial functions in one variable, defining property P as those that are preserved under composition. Specifically, we identify a subset of property P that we call "prime composition property," characterized by polynomials f such that if g(h(x)) equals x for some polynomial g, then either f is a constant function or its decomposition includes a factor of the form h(bx+c). Ultimately, we establish connections between this property and the factorization of certain polynomial iterates.

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools in the northern hemisphere. The appearance, expansion, and eventual disappearance of these patterns can be attributed to heat transferred from the sun's energy. The atmospheric composition, specifically the abundance of methane, affects temperature readings in the stratosphere, leading to varying patterns of cooling and warming. During Saturn's summer, methane cools in the equatorial region and warms in the polar region. In the northern hemisphere's stratosphere, a polar vortex has begun to form, rooted in the symmetry of Saturn's axis. The formation of this vortex is expected to influence the surrounding atmospheric conditions, primarily the temperature readings in the hexagon region. Consequently, the hexagon's temperature readings in the northern hemisphere's stratosphere exhibit warming trends during the summer months. The warming trend in the hexagon is more pronounced in the northern hemisphere's stratosphere than in the polar auroral region, indicating that the polar vortex's formation contributes to the warming trend.

We investigate the exterior of a convex obstacle $U$ in three-dimensional space and prove that solutions to the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation outside $U$ with initial data in the form of a nonlinear self-similar explosion will eventually take the shape of that self-similar solution within a finite period of time. Additionally, if the surface of the obstacle is smooth and the self-similar solution does not cross the concave portion of $U$, we find that the solution remains inside $U$ for a certain period of time.
We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the rational numbers have an infinite number of distinct forms.

We create a linearization functor for full linearization that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Our analysis defines the image of the full linearization functor, resulting in a subcategory of k-fold vector bundles. These vector bundles are equipped with symmetric morphisms associated with the symmetric group Sn. A significant level of structure is added to the image of the full linearization functor, thereby preventing the functors of pullback and pushforward from being exact within the image of the full linearization functor. Therefore, we introduce a notion of polarization for such added structure, aiming to simplify the image of the full linearization functor to the greatest extent possible while maintaining the minimal necessary level of structure, thereby preventing the functors of pullback and pushforward from being exact.

Given a locally compact group G and a compact subset omega of G, this work establishes the equivalence of two expressions that calculate the relationship between orbital integrals and the adjusted measure on omega. These expressions, which take the form of an operator that calculates the relationship between an integral over orbits within G/K by means of the right translation by a element within omega and the adjusted measure on omega, for a fixed maximal compact subgroup K of G, are shown to be equal through a series of computations. Alternatively, this equality can be derived from a more general result that compares the operator to an average of the right translation by a single element within omega and is valid for any measure on omega.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element method combining traditional finite elements and virtual elements, to model single-phase Darcy flow within highly heterogeneous porous media that includes fractures. We specifically develop and test a new VEM approach for our method, implementing it in a way that allows for the inclusion of fractures modeled using boundary interfaces. We also establish the convergence of our method and calculate its associated error. To validate our method, we conduct a series of numerical experiments featuring various test cases, including examples with real-world data. Our results indicate that our method maintains accuracy and flexibility when handling complex geometries and diverse fracture types.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis in practice is often hindered by the need to accurately calculate posterior Bayes factors from Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) estimates, which can be influenced by various factors, including the effectiveness of algorithmic choices, the quality of random number generation, and the robustness of inference resulting from limited data. Furthermore, a universally accepted standard for Bayes factor calculations has not been established, leading to potential concerns about methodological equivalency. To address these challenges, this study examined the impact of distinct algorithmic approaches, such as Laplace-Metropolis approximation and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, on posterior Bayes factor estimates using Bayesian cognitive modeling of an perceptual decision-making task. Our results revealed that while different algorithms yielded similar estimates of the Bayes factor, they did so through distinct means, with implications for their respective assumptions about the underlying process and the structure of the cognitive model. Additionally, we found that the choice of algorithm could influence the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates, with consequences for the required length of simulations. Ultimately, our research highlighted the importance of thoroughly testing the robustness of Bayes factor estimates before comparing cognitive models, and we discussed the potential risks and benefits of various algorithmic approaches in the context of Bayes factor calculations.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an already established semantic connection. Such a model can be utilized for interpreting the predicted relationships between sentences. It can also be employed for the automated analysis of discourse indicators in constructed text samples. This paper presents a trained model and an automated analysis tool called DiscSense which enables users to input a set of sentences and automatically analyze the predicted relationships between their semantic connections, identified corresponding discourse indicators, and the implied semantics.

We investigate a matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and interpretive constraints, analyzing the problem's landscape from a Riemannian perspective. By applying a geometric quotient, we transform the problem into an equivalent and computationally more feasible version involving a sum of square matrices and psd constraints. Through this transformation, we gain insights into the problem's landscape, demonstrating global geodesic convexity and therefore optimality and uniqueness of the solution.

A graph is considered edge-bipartite if its edges can be divided into two disjoint subsets, with each subset forming a clique within the graph. A counterexample, the Grunbaum graph, is presented to demonstrate that there is no consistent algorithm for determining if a given graph is edge-bipartite, when this property is checked using a 2-variable formula. Furthermore, the Grunbaum graph is shown to be a part of a more general class of cubic, non-vertex-transitive, edge-bipartite graphs, displaying properties such as maximal degree, even vertex size, and an abundance of distinct clique sizes.

We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific approach as well as general statistical analysis, our results showed that "social" learning versions resulted in an ergodic Markov Chain, characterized by frequent occurrence of states leading to NE play in the stationary distribution. In contrast, "individual learning" failed to reach the NE state in our simulations, exhibited significantly greater distance from the desired NE state, required substantially longer time to reach the NE state, and displayed reduced robustness. Ultimately, our findings confirmed that the majority of games reached a Nash Equilibrium when players used the "social" learning algorithms.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish that the symbolic and typical power lengths of $I(\mathcal{D})$ are identical, with this equivalence extending to the usual power length when $\mathcal{D}$ holds no loops and exhibits a tree-like structure. Furthermore, in the loop-free and tree-like cases, the typical power length of $I(\mathcal{D})$ is found to be equal to the maximum of the in-degrees found within $\mathcal{D}$.

To create more efficient and dependable AI systems, it is essential to ensure that neural networks can operate reliably even when hardware errors occur. To achieve this, we propose a novel framework called Activation Range Supervision (ARS) that provides a safety guarantee for neural network hardware resilience. Our framework involves training a supporting network to generate precise bounds for each neural network activation, using the fact that neural network outputs are differentiable with respect to activation upper and lower bounds. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ARS by applying it to the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, using the ResNet architecture. Our results show that ARS achieves a high accuracy of 97.86% and 80.19% for MNIST and CIFAR-10 respectively, and can be combined with existing error detection and correction techniques to enhance the reliability of neural network systems.

Building upon the Jordanian twist concept, we have derived a novel type of twist, referred to as a higher-order Jordanian twist, which can be viewed as a member of a parameterized family sharing a common fundamental characteristic. By employing this parameterized family, we have obtained specific expressions for higher-order Jordanian twists in both 1-dimensional and N-dimensional spaces. Furthermore, the derived formulas demonstrate that these higher-order Jordanian twists can be represented as iterated applications of their 1-dimensional counterparts.

Our proposed method, ClusterConsWE, creates a unified semantic space that caters to multiple languages by ensuring that similar words share the same semantic characteristics across each individual language. We achieve this by using style-aware variations of word embeddings for each language and then aligning them using cluster-consistent embeddings that respect the inherent structure of language clusters. Our innovation enables the incorporation of rich linguistic information, including syntactic patterns and dependencies, into the multi-lingual semantic space. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to multiple tasks and across diverse languages, including English, Spanish, Chinese, and Arabic. The results show substantial gains in accuracy across various benchmarks and tasks, including text classification, sentiment analysis, and machine translation.

The publicly available data for 2017 Xe-Xe collision runs at the LHC, totaling 12.2 micro-barn inverse combinations, were utilized to investigate transverse momentum distributions of pions, kaons, protons, and phi mesons in both medium- and high-energy ranges. Pion data in the low-energy range were compared to theoretical predictions based on isobar models, revealing discrepancies with the predicted sizes of rho mesons. Middle-collosion energy data for kaons and protons showed that their momentum distributions are consistent with theoretical predictions based on relativistic viscous fluid dynamics, with estimated viscosity-to-entropy ratios of 1.9 plus or minus 0.9 and 1.04 plus or minus 0.30 for the two energies.

This research paper examines the dynamics of the 2019 Chilean protests by integrating elements of civil unrest, ethnic diversity, and economic inequality into an epidemiological model that accounts for spatial interactions. It analyzes how protest participation and violence are influenced by ethnic minority status and economic conditions, and it specifies the corresponding parameters in the model. It then leverages statistical techniques to estimate the model's parameters based on aggregate data from 54 Chilean municipalities. The model's predictions are compared to actual protest data, and it shows promise in forecasting violence and overall protest participation across the municipalities.

This research develops an innovative approach for addressing constraints containing the character '*' in regular expressions over symbols, by establishing a connection to a more general problem involving the character '*' in regular expressions over sets. We demonstrate that determining whether a regular expression with the character '*' in its context is satisfiable is equivalent to determining whether a specific type of regular expression without the character '*' is satisfiable, and we achieve this result by creating a relationship with the more general problem of validating the satisfiability of regular expressions with the character '*' in their context, which was previously solved by Malischk and Wendelin. By extending their prior solution, we develop an iterative algorithm for solving the original problem, and we also provide an alternative solution using a regular expression transducer. Additionally, we identify a connection between the original problem and the validation of regular expression inversions, which was previously solved by an iterative algorithm and a non-deterministic finite automaton, and we further discovered a connection between regular expression inversions and regular expression transducers, which has not been previously reported.

Our proposed method, EMA-VIO, leverages the strengths of both visual-inertial odometry and external memory attention to enable a single RE-ID model to be utilized across various environments, thereby bypassing the need for training on diverse indoor datasets. In a thorough evaluation, covering numerous public VIO localization benchmarks and an expansive indoor dataset, our results demonstrate substantial gains in accuracy, particularly in areas with minimal textural information, along with improved robustness to various challenging scenarios.

A novel concept, quadratic topological order, has been introduced to describe a specific type of quantum phase that occurs in exotic materials and systems, distinguished from ordinary topological order by an essential difference in dimensionality. Theoretical models demonstrating quadratic topological order are scarce and primarily existing theories either approximate or miss essential details. In our research, we develop an exhaustive framework for Weyl materials of all orders, including a novel category we call square-root higher-order Weyl materials, and thoroughly examine their topological characteristics through both theoretical and experimental means. A strategy is also proposed to achieve a comprehensive understanding of these systems by applying group theory alone, without the need for extensive numerical computations. Our findings are further validated through actual numerical computations of our proposed model.

This study focuses on numerically resolving the solution to the inverse problem of determining a time-varying current within a conductor using measurements of the magnetic field outside the conductor, without direct access to the exterior region where the field is affected by the conductor. A non-iterative, quasi-reversibility approach is developed to address this problem, and the corresponding numerical strategy is designed to solve the resulting system of equations. Key aspects of the numerical scheme, including stability, convergence, and computational efficiency, are established through theoretical and practical verification. Furthermore, the method is applied to a 2D problem where the current varies over time, and to a 3D problem with constant, time-invariant currents.

In the context of multi-agent systems, knowledge exchange is a common operation between agents, where an agent selects and shares part of its knowledge with others. This exchange aims to combine their joint knowledge. The primary challenge lies in determining the portion of knowledge to be shared, as unnecessary information exchange can lead to data management difficulties. To address this issue, an approach called Federated Selective Collection of Knowledge was proposed, consisting of two stages: in the initial stage, agents share parts of their knowledge based on individual interests; in the second stage, the shared knowledge is combined using set operations. The result is a joint knowledge base that is both comprehensive and manageable. Furthermore, this approach prevents unwanted information exchange during data collection, thus providing federated privacy protection.

We analyze the Mordell-Weil rank growth of a specific family of elliptic curves obtained through quartic extensions in the rational numbers. These extensions are defined by irreducible polynomials with coefficients given by symmetric and alternating extensions of the rational numbers, specifically in the symmetric group $S_4$ and the alternating group $A_4$. By utilizing the approach of Gross and Zagier, we determine the rank of an elliptic curve at a particular point in time and track its progression. Along the way, we provide a detailed explanation of the method, including an examination of the rank within the context of quartic Legendre elliptic curves.

A crucial aspect of quantum states is the non-entanglement area principle, which describes the relationship between the amount of information that cannot be shared between two regions within a system and the surface defining those regions. A key derivative concept is the quantum null energy complex, an expression related to the change in von Neumann entropy across a null surface in relation to the change in area, with its bound providing insights into the non-entanglement area principle. Our research focuses on the quantum null energy complex within holographic theories, where we calculate its derivative for an arbitrary spacetime geometry and then apply it to the study of holographic entanglement. Furthermore, we establish an inequality based on the non-entanglement area principle, bounding the change in entanglement entropy across a null surface by the change in its associated area. This inequality holds under the assumption that the null surface is within a specific type of spacetime geometry known as AdS-dS.

We investigate quantum systems whose initial and final states are both within a specified sphere centered on a symmetric point within a seven-dimensional space, specifically within the context of spin-1 particles. Our primary focus is on identifying distinct criteria, including the Neumann-Bacher, Dirac, and asymmetric purities, as well as their corresponding bounding expressions, particularly the optimal quantum speed limit for asymmetric purities. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the relationship between these conditions and their impact on the duration required to transition between initial and final states. Our study demonstrates that when the initial state is not orthogonal to the final state, the most stringent condition is the Neumann-Bacher criterion, which in turn surpasses the Dirac and asymmetric purities conditions. Conversely, when the initial state is orthogonal to the final state, the most stringent condition shifts to the asymmetric purities criterion. Notably, the optimal quantum speed limit for asymmetric purities exceeds the other conditions, making it the most restrictive bound in all scenarios.

The article investigates the metric properties of a specific operator, the (Riesz) interpolation projector associated with the subspace $M\subset L^p(\mu)$, where $1<p<\infty$. It is shown that if $M$ is a subspace of $L^p(\mu)$ with which it has a continuous embedding, then the projector operator is continuous with respect to the norm, and thus it is also continuously embedded in the space $L^q(\mu)$ for $1<q<\infty$. It is also demonstrated that there exists a constant $C$ such that the property $\|T\|_{L^p(\mu)\rightarrow L^q(\mu)}\leq C$ holds. It is noteworthy that the nature of this constant is not arbitrary, as it can be determined based on the characteristic properties of the space $M$ and the measure $\mu$. It is also proven that this constant is a part of the best possible assessment for the norm of the projector operator. Additionally, the article provides specific examples to illustrate the nature of this constant in various scenarios.

A key limitation of superconducting quantum circuits is the difficulty in pinpointing sources of leakage, given the high sensitivity of their output to minor changes, as a result of their intricate geometry. Identifying the causes of radiation, which could be both useful, through self-monitoring, or detrimental, by hindering the performance or causing diachronic degradation, requires non-invasive analysis. A non-contact, optical method to localize and examine the current distribution using terahertz near-field microscopy is presented, demonstrating the detection of previously unknown pathways of radiation in a Josephson chip. Furthermore, this approach is used to investigate radiation patterns in resonators with integrated antennas, enabling the retrieval of essential information about their parameters and facilitating proper alignment of quantum elements with respect to their classical counterparts.

Our research explores the long-term evolution of the Venusian atmosphere, examining the significance of various processes that have shaped its development over time. We have identified key processes including cloud layer condensate feedback, sulfur cycle feedback, OH radical destruction, and aerosol impact on atmospheric escape. We have also established the relationships among them. To understand the historical atmosphere of Venus, we have established a framework for analysis through a series of figure diagrams. Each figure provides a distinct historical perspective, from the early Earth-like atmosphere of Venus to its present state. We have further explored the atmosphere's current state and future evolution, offering predictions for its development over the next few billion years. Our research indicates that the processes affecting the Venusian atmosphere have remained relatively constant throughout its history, despite the atmosphere's composition changing over time. We believe this invariance is critical, as it has allowed us to establish equations describing the atmosphere's evolution for the next few billion years. Our predictions for the atmosphere's future evolution include a runaway snowball Earth scenario in about 10 billion years, following which the atmosphere will return to a quasi-stable state similar to its current condition.

Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, which are otherwise challenging to determine, especially in the case of multiple point processes. By utilizing the stationary distribution of the process, we established a theoretical framework for our method's accuracy. Through simulated data and real-world examples, including an analysis of online message replies, we have shown that this method compares favorably to other estimation methods, including maximum likelihood and variational Bayesian approximation.

As high-powered lasers interact with matter, their behavior becomes increasingly complex and difficult to predict, necessitating thorough research into the interplay of electromagnetic fields and matter. The dynamics of laser pulses interacting with a certain type of plasma, where the electrons move at a speed comparable to the light speed, necessitate the use of relativistic techniques to model the plasma's response effectively. According to recent research, a specific plasma structure can alter the laser pulses' polarization while increasing their power, even to the point of changing linearly polarized pulses to circularly polarized ones. The study delves into the physics underlying this phenomenon, demonstrating that a change in the plasma structure can lead to a shift from linear to circular polarization, resulting in an increase in the power of linearly polarized pulses, with powers exceeding $10^{23}$ W. The findings are further validated using a different numerical method, with the results presented in a way that connects them to the underlying physics.

Using form-factor approaches and the known properties of the tau lepton, we calculate the electric dipole moment magnitude by considering various contributions from lightweights, heavies, and a combination of virtual particles. Our research encompasses three scenarios based on the unknown light quark and lepton properties within the Standard Model or beyond. We examine the relationships between the tau's electric dipole moment and other low-energy processes, including $J/\psi$ and $\tau$ decays, as well as Higgs and $\tau$ interactions. We also explore implications for the anomalous $Z$ and $W$ decays and the $\tau$-induced Higgs contribution within the Standard Model.

We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, and \cite{Dobrev:1977pv}, we revisit the concept of spinning conformal field theory block operators in two-dimensional conformal field theories. Here, these block operators are associated with primary fields that possess half-integer spin and are situated within a specific range of the central charge spectrum. We establish that a particular combination of conformal field theory Weyl operators can be linked to a specific block operator through a third operator, which itself can be identified as a descendant field. Furthermore, we demonstrate that descendant fields can be constructed using a conformal field theory stress tensor, in addition to other conformal field theory Weyl operators, by applying a sequence of differential operators to the identity operator. Notably, when working within a conformally extended AdS$_{3}$ spacetime, these descendant fields can be associated with spinning primary field block operators in Liouville theory and Liouville-like theories within the AdS$_{3}$ CFT$_{2}$ correspondence.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson proposed the combinatorial Pontrjagin classes for a generic morphism, claiming it as a significant alternative to the Whitehead torsion, and demonstrated their equivalence in the context of a regular graph that forms a triangle. We have expanded on their work by providing the combinatorial Pontrjagin classes for a broader class of regular graphs, specifically those without three-fold vertices, and showed these are equal to the classical Pontrjagin classes.

We analyzed the optical and near-infrared light curves and spectra of SN~2020jfo, a supernova exhibiting a rare and short luminosity plateau phase. By re-examining the light curves with a new method that removes systematic errors, we determined the duration of the plateau phase to be approximately 13 days. SN~2020jfo is only the second known Type II-S supernova within a sample of 160 Type II supernovae in a specific galaxy type group that has a short plateau duration. We also found that SN~2020jfo shares similar explosion and ejecta properties with the SN~1999gb, and that its light curves can be fit with a two-component model consisting of a standard Type II supernova component and a component resembling that of an extreme supernova. Furthermore, we propose an alternative explanation for the short plateau duration based on an extreme supernova interaction with a massive hydrogen-rich companion star in a galaxy with an elevated star formation rate.

To enhance the efficiency of wide-field X-ray monitoring with lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a spatial modulation technique that involves a array of LE optics with varying pitch distances. By utilizing a comb filter with a periodic pattern mirroring the arrangement of the LE optics, we can distinguish the origin of signals within the two-dimensional field of the LE array. This technique allows us to identify transverse displacement of optical images across the detector, enabling the recovery of spatial information outside the field of a single LE optic. This process results in a solid signal-to-noise ratio for signals with a signal-to-noise ratio greater than 10, facilitating the deconvolution of images from the LE optics. Via simulations and actual observations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in achieving a modulation transfer function of 0.25 or higher and the successful detection of known X-ray sources with a flux limit of less than 1.02 x 10^-13 erg s^-1 cm^-2.
We provide the level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity, a concept introduced by Sylvain Raulay-Nghèt, and demonstrate its relevance through the study of a specific PDE.

To explore the connection between dark matter and baryonic matter within a system, we use two tools: the distribution function and the speed field. While the former describes spatial patterns, the latter addresses velocity patterns. Investigating the speed field through machine learning, our convolutional neural network analyzes dark matter simulation data and directly maps velocity distributions onto spatial distributions. By employing this approach, we observed that the speed field is intertwined with the distribution function through a nonlinear relationship. To gain further insight, we broken down this connection into three separate components and discovered unique relationships for each component. Furthermore, we found that the speed field influences the distribution function through an asymmetrical non-linear interaction. To incorporate this finding into the equation of dark matter evolution, we developed an expressive neural network operator that accurately predicts the evolution equation's solution. Through additional analysis, we demonstrated that the speed field's structure remains unchanged across varying initial conditions and that its evolution is characterized by a self-similar pattern.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. Our method, which builds on the success of the "rotating star in a rotating coordinate system" concept, utilizes a non-standard set of coordinates centered on the star. We calculate the star's total angular momentum and its rate of change through the conservation of angular momentum in these coordinates. Our numerical approach consists of two main components: the first part solves the Einstein equations in the standard rotating coordinate system; the second part solves the angular momentum conservation equation for the coordinates of the star. We have applied and tested our method by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity through an iterative process, where we calculate the angular velocity at the surface using the conservation of angular momentum in the coordinates of the star. We have further demonstrated the accuracy of our method by comparing these configurations directly to numerical solutions available in the field.

A major challenge in creating AI models that extract information from documents is the time-consuming and labor-intensive process of labeling data. To make document AI more accessible to a broader range of organizations, we're exploring a key idea: it's possible to significantly decrease the cost of data labeling by limiting the amount of information required for annotations. In a study involving models for extracting data from business documents in multiple languages, we found that only labeling a small set of 100 documents, which accounted for just 1 percent of the total data, was sufficient to achieve comparable performance to models trained on full data sets annotated at length. This reduction in labeling costs was consistent across various models and evaluation metrics.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the identification of signals emanating from neutron stars within the cleaned data of compact binaries. Currently, this task is accomplished using matched filtering with models predicted from general relativity. As future detectors enhance in sensitivity and future sky surveys yield more data, the volume of data that needs to be analyzed through matched filtering will significantly increase, leading to computational challenges. To overcome these, we developed an alternate method using deep learning, specifically a convolutional neural network, that can identify neutron stars based on their component masses with a 94% accuracy and distinguish between binary neutron star and neutron star-black hole events with a 99% accuracy.

Urban diversity refers to the coexistence of various community elements such as economic statuses within a city. Research suggests that economic status segregation in a city is not beneficial for its citizens, as it can lead to heightened aggression, crime, social isolation, and decreased civic participation. The COVID-19 pandemic brought about significant changes in how people interact with each other in public spaces, with face mask regulations and social distancing measures leading to increased solitude and reduced public engagement. To understand the impact of these changes on urban diversity, our study analyzed data from a large American city gathered before the pandemic and over the course of a year into the pandemic. The data, which tracked people's interactions in public places based on income groups, revealed that the pandemic worsened income diversity in urban encounters by increasing the distance between economic status groups. Consequently, this further exacerbated economic status segregation in the city.

Three-dimensional simulations of massive star formation, considering both accretion and episodic accretion, reveal that even in the presence of magnetic fields, which help prevent spin-down and prompt collapse, a distinguishing characteristic emerges when the total mass accumulates at a rapid rate exceeding $10^{-4} \mbox{~M}_\sun \mbox{yr}^{-1}$. Here, a distinct accumulation period begins where massive protostars quickly gather mass in discrete, massive episodes rather than through a steady flow. During this period, the overall mass grows in a fragmented and clumpy manner due to reflections from nearby molecules like HCO$^+$. As a result, an intriguing scenario emerges where multiple protostars with total masses above $30 \mbox{~M}_\sun$ merge and then continue their development, potentially influencing the characteristics of the resulting stars.

This research investigates how a rotating water surface, in the form of waves resulting from an initial disturbance, evolves over time, particularly in deep water with the aid of the Hamiltonian approach. Through the Hamiltonian method, we derive a new Dysthe equation describing the dynamics of waves in rotating deep water. This new equation differs from its non-rotating counterpart and demonstrates similar characteristics, specifically the appearance of a constant mean flow term and the distinct behavior of wave energy as it relates to the peak amplitude. Furthermore, we demonstrate the Hamiltonian formulation's value by applying it to a set of exact conservation laws, and we analytically determine the wave energy's expression in the deep water limit.

In the context of locally convex spaces, particularly those with a characteristic that their spaces of distributions are well-behaved under mild assumptions, we develop the concept of differential forms that vary smoothly and evaluate them using the Stokes formula. The paper also introduces an operator that reduces the regularity of differential forms at the cost of introducing a compact support.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing environments is a complex task for robots, whose success relies heavily on advanced sensing, sophisticated control systems, and efficient computational power. This paper focuses on a key aspect of navigation, namely path planning, and presents a novel method for integrating sensory data from a limited field-of-view sonar. By utilizing a layered control structure, the approach ensures seamless integration with existing navigation systems. A key benefit of the proposed method is the significant reduction it achieves in the computational demands associated with path planning, without compromising safety standards. In addition to providing a detailed mathematical explanation, a simulation environment has been created to demonstrate the proposed algorithm's efficacy, and a real-world test is also conducted to compare its performance with an established method.

The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by relying on engagement metrics that favor sensational and unusual content. In order to counter this surge, automated methods for false news detection have been proposed and implemented. These methods typically take the form of machine learning models, deep neural networks, and hybrid systems. In contrast to traditional approaches that focus on false news classification, this study presents a novel idea of utilizing text summarization to distinguish true from false news. The study's key achievement is the development of three unique text summarization models, namely TF-IDF, HSA, and BART, that outperform the majority of existing false news classification systems according to the evaluation metrics. Additionally, the study introduces a new evaluation metric called summary-based relevance, which assesses the relevance of summarized news to its original content. The findings are supported by a large-scale dataset consisting of 100,000 news summaries across multiple categories.

We investigate the bending effect within Gaussian random fields, specifically
the phenomenon where the most curved level sets of a random function are
most likely to take on the most extreme values from either end of the
function's range.  We approach this analytically by examining the distribution
of the minimum number of levels sets that contain the most extreme values,
naming this number the level set's extremity.  We derive the distributional
form of the most curved level sets' extremity, and in doing so, gain insight
into the relationship between curvature, the function's second derivative, and
the extremity.  The most curved level sets' extremity is found to be the
smallest integer greater than a half integer, when the function's range is
normalized to the interval $[-1,1]$.  We further investigate the relationship
between curvature and the function's endpoints, deriving the distribution of the
difference between the values of the function at the most curved level sets
and the most extreme values within those sets.  The results we obtain are
relevant to the bending effect, but also address the problem of estimating the
interval containing the values of the function within its most curved level sets.

We develop a new iterative method for finding the principal component of a data matrix whose entries are subject to random masking, while ensuring rotational invariance. This results in a relaxation of the traditional $\ell_1$-norm PCA, yet we demonstrate that the proposed method yields an estimate equivalent to the masked data, up to a specific rotation. Our algorithm leverages an iterative reweighting approach and an approximate proximal operator, and we prove that it converges linearly to the desired solution. When applied to randomly generated data, it yields an estimate for the principal component that matches the true value with high precision, outperforming the standard singular value decomposition rotation-based estimation method.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In the realm of affective computing, semantic annotation is a critical task that requires the attribution of emotion-related semantic roles to query strings. Following the release of a prior study on this subject, researchers received a set of annotated data containing emotion-related questions along with corresponding semantic role structures. In the presented work, research is focused on assessing the validity of this annotation as well as identifying any discrepancies that may arise due to the initial training data and research design. Further analysis is conducted to rectify the identified issues and test the resulting data against alternative research designs.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system to match their local observations with the global environment is crucial. We present HiTMap, a novel spatial representation concept consisting of interconnected triangle maps to achieve this goal. Each triangle within the representation corresponds to a distinct location within the environment, with corresponding point-cloud observations. The unique feature of HiTMap is the hierarchical structure of the triangles, where each triangle is matched against the point-cloud observations from a specific location, accurately capturing the spatial relationships between them. We have implemented a navigation system using HiTMap in an unknown environment, with a PX4 autopilot system on a flying robot, that autonomously builds the map and makes navigation decisions based on the surrounding obstacle information. Our results show that this system can efficiently navigate around obstacles and accurately build the map with minimal errors.

One of the most sensitive techniques for detecting changes in local gravitational fields also offers the ability to accurately measure local magnetic fields. By leveraging the connection between gravitational and electromagnetic fields as described by Einstein's general relativity and Maxwell's theory, atomic interferometry can successfully pick up variations in magnetic fields through the effect they have on light interacting with matter. Specifically, by measuring the shift in a light beam's frequency resulting from the interaction between light and matter, atomic interferometry can reach an incredible level of precision equivalent to detecting changes in gravitational fields of about 1 cm per second squared. This already impressive level of sensitivity can be further enhanced to a level of precision equivalent to detecting changes in magnetic fields of about 10 nT per second, making it the most precise measurement of magnetic field variations ever achieved.

In this work, a classical mixture model is reimagined using stochastic processes and geometric methods. We reinterpret mixtures as expectations calculated over the distribution of a random set, specifically an element of a mixture space defined by independent components. We show that modeling such sets as second-order stationary random fields allows us to derive an analytical formulation for the density of any component, which in turn enables us to determine the distribution of the set itself. We demonstrate that this formulation results in the well-known kernel density estimation mixture model density when the set's characteristics can be characterized as having a uniform distribution. Moreover, this approach is adaptable for modeling complex data sets by incorporating feature spaces similar to kernel density estimation.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices like GPUs relies heavily on efficient memory access and optimal data layout. Despite this, current CUDA standards lack a high-performance allocator for dynamic memory allocation. To overcome this limitation, we present DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator that provides automatic memory compaction and sorting through a block-based, coarse-grained reordering of memory blocks. DynaSOAr also offers advanced features such as real-time tracking of memory blocks, detailed memory access statistics, and the ability to sort memory blocks based on various criteria. We evaluated DynaSOAr on real-world applications showing that it achieves performance gains of up to 3 times and is particularly effective in scenarios requiring memory compaction and sorting on the order of hundreds of kilobytes.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn clusters on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of a single Mn adatom, the YSR state formation was examined over a range of distances from the surface, while Mn clusters were found to exhibit ferromagnetic behavior and their properties can be tailored through arrangement and spacing.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, we determined the star's characteristics, revealing it to be a young G-type star with a mass similar to that of the Sun and a radius 10% greater than the Sun's. As a member of the $\gamma$ Persei young star group, TOI-712 is estimated to be approximately 480 million years old. Through a spectroscopic analysis of its spectrum, we found its stellar atmosphere to have a surface temperature around 5800K, making it a habitable zone boundary. By studying the star's luminosity, we calculated its mass and radius to be 0.83 times the mass and radius of the Sun, respectively. Further research revealed that TOI-712 is a metal-rich star with a slight abundance of metals in its atmosphere. By studying the planet's phases, we determined the orbital planes of the four planets to be aligned with each other, suggesting the planets may have formed from a single disk. With the discovery of four planets around TOI-712, we found an Earth-sized planet called TOI-712b, a mini-Neptune called TOI-712.01, another mini-Neptune called TOI-712.02, and a super-Earth called

We examined the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, keeping the experimental structure of TiO2 in mind.  Our results showed that N anti-site defects are magnetically stable in isolation but lose their magnetism when paired with oxygen vacancies, whereas C anti-site defects remain nonmagnetic across all scenarios.  Moreover, N-filled octahedral interstitial sites exhibit magnetic characteristics but only when paired with oxygen vacancies, whereas C-filled interstitial sites do not display any magnetic properties.  Our study discovered that both N and C defects can exhibit spin-glass behavior when paired with titanium anti-site defects.  Notably, N dopants demonstrate minimal host disorder compared to carbon, and all scenarios are feasible regardless of how the N is incorporated (interstitial or anti-site).  Our research also analyzed the energy differences associated with these defects and identified that the most low-cost pathway involves introducing N anti-site defects or N-filled octahedral interstitial sites via the formation of TiO2_N2 or TiO2_CN2 aliovalent compounds, respectively.

In order to improve the measurement of the top quark's properties and elastic top quark production measurements at the Large Hadron Collider, a new variable is proposed that combines information from the missing transverse energy and the rapidity gap between two protons scattering off each other. This variable, referred to as the "elastic energy," could significantly reduce background sources such as fake missing transverse energy and proton-proton scattering off nucleon-rich nuclei. It is anticipated that the identification of the most prominent peaks in the elastic energy spectrum, resulting from the creation of top quark pairs through the self-energy of protons, will yield highly reliable and precise top quark pair production cross-section measurements, with estimated uncertainties of 5-10%.

In the context of graph theory, an ordering of a graph refers to a sequence of its vertices generated through a specific rule. We examine the properties of ordering generated from tournament-like graphs, specifically focusing on a concept called upper richness, and its related Ramsey theory implications. A key finding demonstrates that upper richness in tournament-like graphs corresponds to a more general concept, known as minimal degree, which also serves as a necessary condition for the property of being able to generate a rich ordering through a certain method. Furthermore, we establish an ineqaulity linking the smallest possible cardinality of a subset whose existence guarantees a specific property in a certain type of Ramsey theory to the largest possible cardinality of another type of subset. A previous result by Erdos, Spence, and Brown is generalized through this inequality.

Our analysis highlights that qutrits based on Ising-type spins exhibit significantly
greater tolerance for errors made during the course of computation. Specifically,
we found that qutrits-based systems can function effectively within a broader
range of variation in their annealing schedules, are less affected by noise
targeted at the transverse field component, and are more resistant to certain
types of amplitude damping. Furthermore, we determined that the optimal annealing
schedule rates that minimize error outside the parameter regime recommended
for experimental safety still yield practical results for a variety of scenarios.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through the interaction of highly intense and short duration gamma-ray beams with thin solid targets, specifically in environments where QED dominates. Studies focusing on solid-state targets, particularly two-dimensional semiconductor films, have revealed that positrons are generated at remarkably high rates, with estimates suggesting they could surpass the generated amount of electrons in the far field. A model based on analytical and semi-analytical calculations demonstrates that in the limit of intense fields, positrons are produced at rates comparable to electrons, with estimates in the order of 10% of the generated amount of electrons in the far field. Furthermore, research implies that high rates of polarized positrons can be achieved with two-dimensional semiconductor films, with rates in the order of 10% of the generated amount of electrons in the far field. A proposed facility featuring a gamma-ray beamline with an energy range between 10 and 300 MeV and an intensity range between 10 and 10^4 GW/cm^2 with a focal spot of approximately 10 micrometers in diameter is also discussed.

Given a finite group G and a subgroup H of G, we examine the function f(n) that represents the number of n-length words in FN(H) that do not correspond to elements of G. It is proved that if this function has a polynomial ceiling for all positive integer lengths n, then it implies that the index of H in G is finite. Consequently, we establish that having a superpolynomial number of distinct coset representatives to H in G is a necessary condition for the exponent of a finite group to contain at least two prime factors.

This research develops a precise temperature detection capability in a highly energy-efficient and adaptable design, suitable for use in advanced microcontrollers and low-power systems across a broad voltage range. The proposed temperature detector employs a bandgap and thermal voltage reference source in its structure, allowing it to operate across a wide voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V without the need for additional voltage conversion. The design leverages subthreshold operation and multiple threshold voltages to achieve adaptable operation and reduced power consumption.
